metadata.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national mistakenly deported from the U.S., arrives in Spain

sources.news_title: ‘Free of everything evil’: Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks out from Spain, after fleeing US
sources.text:
‘Free of everything evil’: Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks out from Spain, after fleeing US
Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks to people who held a prayer vigil and rally on his behalf outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in Baltimore, Maryland, on Aug. 25, 2025. Lydia Walther Rodriguez with CASA interprets for him. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
WASHINGTON — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the wrongly deported immigrant who fought the Trump administration’s efforts to re-deport him to one of several African nations, said Wednesday that he felt joyful to choose to voluntarily depart from the United States to Spain.
“I feel happy,” Abrego Garcia said in Spanish, shortly after arriving in Madrid. “I feel free, free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point.”
The federal government agreed to allow Abrego Garcia, a longtime Maryland resident, to voluntarily leave the U.S. for Spain late Tuesday, apparently concluding a 20-month legal saga that cast a national spotlight on the president’s aggressive deportation campaign after Abrego Garcia was erroneously deported to a brutal Salvadoran prison.
He appeared during a Wednesday virtual press conference with the immigration advocacy group that has spearheaded his case, We Are CASA.
“The government did not decide where my story continues,” Abrego Garcia said. “My family and I decided.”
One of his attorneys, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said Abrego Garcia’s time in Spain would be temporary and that he plans to wait for a new administration to take office before making an effort to return to the U.S. His wife and their three children remain in Maryland.
He is in Spain on a tourist visa, which lasts for about 90 days, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. He declined to give details about where Abrego Garcia would go next after his tourist visa expires.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said because Abrego Garcia is married to a U.S. citizen, there is a legal avenue they could pursue, but in order for Abrego Garcia to be allowed back into the country, he’ll need a certain waiver from the State Department.
A U.S. citizen married to a noncitizen can petition for a visa for their spouse, which could eventually lead to a green card, or lawful permanent residence.
“It is going to be up to the next administration to reunite this family as quickly as possible and to bring Mr. Abrego Garcia back to Maryland, but this does not require an act of extraordinary executive grace,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “There is an existing immigration pathway.”
‘Any country that is willing to accept him’
The federal judge overseeing his case, Paula Xinis, on Wednesday unsealed a court order from Oct. 6, where Abrego Garcia’s attorneys and Department of Justice lawyers agreed to let Abrego Garcia self-deport from the U.S. “to any country that is willing to accept him,” with a date set for Nov. 24.
In self-deportation, the government makes life so difficult for people without legal status that they choose to leave. The Trump administration has pressured immigrants to self-deport by offering monetary incentives or threatening to levy hefty fines or detention against those who don’t leave on their own.
Because U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement kept Abrego Garcia’s passport after he was released from immigrant detention, he could not leave the country without permission from the federal government. As part of a condition of his release from detention, he was also placed on electronic monitoring.
In the October order, Xinis ordered federal immigration agents to remove Abrego Garcia’s ankle monitor before he was set to board his flight to Madrid, and remove any prohibitions that blocked him from leaving the U.S., such as a no-fly list.
On Wednesday, in a separate order, Xinis, dissolved all injunctions that barred the Trump administration from removing him to a third country, finding the case moot after Abrego Garcia left the U.S. on Tuesday.
In a late Tuesday statement, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Trump administration was “delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain.”
Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador to visit Abrego Garcia and advocate for his return to the U.S., said during Wednesday’s press conference that the Trump administration’s efforts to remove him to several African countries was “a vendetta against Kilmar Abrego Garcia because he stood up for his constitutional rights.”
“This is a case where the court system did ultimately work, despite the efforts of the Trump administration to trample over our Constitution, and so this is a good moment,” he said.
Van Hollen added that he met with Spain’s ambassador to the U.S., Ángeles Moreno Bau, and informed her of “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration, the U.S. government, against Kilmar Abrego Garcia.”
Speaking tour next
In the meantime, Abrego Garcia plans to go on a speaking tour in Spain and elsewhere to tell his story of being mistakenly deported in March 2025 to a brutal prison in El Salvador, despite having legal protections that prevented him from being removed to his home country.
He is also expected to relate the legal battles the Trump administration waged against him and the efforts to remove him to several African nations.
While he was at the mega-prison in El Salvador, he said in court filings he experienced physical and psychological torture.
Federal and appeals courts, including the Supreme Court, found he was illegally removed, and the lower courts ordered the Trump administration to return him.
When Abrego Garcia was brought back to the U.S., it was because the Department of Justice charged him with an indictment that stemmed from a traffic stop in Tennessee. A federal judge in Nashville threw out the case, finding that the Department of Justice was being vindictive against Abrego Garcia.
The Department of Justice offered Abrego Garcia a deal that if he pleaded guilty to the Tennessee charges of two counts of human smuggling, he would be allowed to be removed to Costa Rica, but he pleaded not guilty.
For more than a year, he agreed to be removed to Costa Rica, but the Trump administration has tried to remove him to the African nations instead.
Xinis found the Trump administration had not made a good faith effort to remove Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica, which agreed to accept him and give him refugee status. The Trump administration tried to send him to Eswatini, Liberia, Ghana, and Uganda.
Abrego Garcia said his decision to leave the U.S. means that “this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”
Xinis, who oversaw his wrongful deportation case, was also presiding over his second case, where he challenged his immigration detention, known as a habeas corpus claim. She ordered that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement release Abrego Garcia from detention because the agency was not making an effort to remove him, making his detention unlawful.

sources.news_title: NBC’s ‘Today’ Ignores as ABC, CBS Barely Cover Beloved ‘Maryland Man’ Self-Deporting
sources.text:
Despite what’s likely been thousands of minutes on broadcast and cable networks, plus dozens of friendly interviews for his lawyers, it was surprising that late Tuesday and early Wednesday the “Big Three” of ABC, CBS, and NBC paid scant attention on their flagship morning and evening shows to their beloved illegal immigrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia — affectionately referred to as a “Maryland man” — self-deporting to far-left Spain following a nearly two-year legal battle with the Trump administration.
None of the lead evening shows mentioned Garcia’s decision on Tuesday, and Wednesday brought about short news briefs on ABC’s Good Morning America and CBS Mornings that combined for 71 seconds. That means NBC’s top newscasts — Today and NBC Nightly News — have yet to mention this supposedly harmless illegal doing what they had spent years helping Garcia avoid doing.
Interesting: NBC’s ‘Today’ skipped while ABC’s ‘Good Morning America’ and ‘CBS Mornings’ barely covered news of their beloved illegal immigrant — “Maryland man” Kilmar Abrego Garcia — self-deporting to Spain pic.twitter.com/R3kAgaXAqx
— Curtis Houck (@CurtisHouck) November 25, 2026
On ABC, weekend co-host Will Reeve kicked off the second half-hour with the development:
We do have a lot of news to get to here at 7:30, beginning with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was mistakenly deported to a prison in El Salvador by the Trump administration — he’s self-deporting now to Spain. He was seen last night boarding a flight to Madrid. Abrego Garcia was returned to the U.S. after a Supreme Court ruling, but still faced a deportation effort. The Department of Homeland Security said it was “delighted” he had self-deported.
It was the same setup on CBS Mornings. Not only did it lead off its second half-hour string of news briefs, but it was delivered by a weekend co-host in CBS Saturday Morning co-host Adriana Diaz.
Diaz even used the word “mistakenly” at the onset of her 27-second brief: “We begin with an update on Kilmar Abrego Garcia. He’s the man mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his native country of El Salvador. He was later brought back to this country, and now CBS News confirms he has arrived in Spain after leaving the U.S.”
She continued: “In a statement, he says, I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom.’ The Department of Homeland Security posted on social media that Abrego Garcia will ‘never be allowed back in the United States.’”
At the time Abrego Garcia burst onto the scene (and before allegations emerged about domestic abuse and trafficking), he was the toast of newsrooms in New York and Washington as they buried (or mocked) Rachel Morin’s murder (by another illegal immigrant), his wife was treated to a cartoonishly soft interview on GMA and held up as a test case for what Trump was supposedly going to do next to black people en masse.
Today did cover when human smuggling charges were dropped back in May, but they conveniently left out the fact that the presiding judge was a former Democratic donor.
Back to the present, Today had other ideas for news briefs, including the viral images of a Benjamin Franklin impersonator being arrested recently in Boston.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports — and DHS is 'delighted' about it
sources.text:
DHS Sec. Mullin issued a response after Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the US.
The long, bitter saga of Kilmar Abrego Garcia has come to an end after the Salvadoran man self-deported to Spain, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
Garcia, an illegal alien dubbed a "Maryland man" by the press, was nabbed by federal officials in March 2025. While the Trump administration immediately sought his deportation, Democrats instead turned his case into a political and legal campaign against the president's immigration policies.
'He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.'
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin released a statement confirming that Garcia had gone to Spain.
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said Mullin in a DHS press release Tuesday. "We promised the American people that this human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator would not remain in our country. Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans."
The administration originally deported him to the infamous mega-prison in El Salvador for criminal gang members based on the determination that Garcia was an MS-13 gang member. However, he was returned to the U.S. after an order from a federal judge.
Garcia has denied being in MS-13 and engaging in human trafficking, and neither allegation has been proven in court.
After a prolonged court battle related to whether Garcia had due process rights, the administration sought to deport him to Uganda; Eswatini, a small country in Africa; and finally to Ghana.
Garcia's team has confirmed that he left for Spain, CBS News reported.
Many on social media are not sad to see him go.
"Good riddance. Don’t come back you sorry POS," said Republican former West Virginia state Rep. Derrick Evans.
"Thoughts and prayers to the Democratic Party for this loss," responded Libs of TikTok.
"Finally, Kilmar Abrego Garcia is gone. I’ll never understand why democrats wanted this guy here so badly," said another critic on social media.
"Kilmar Abrego Garcia — a criminal who should be in prison — just arrived in Spain and is being treated like a f**king rock star. No justice. No accountability," said another critic.
RELATED: Judge orders release of Kilmar Garcia — but DHS vows that 'he will never go free on American soil'
CBS News reported that he arrived in Madrid, along with his wife, his child, and his attorney. Video shows him having his ankle monitor cut off at an airport.
Garcia said he was happy about moving to Spain.
"In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible," he said, according to CBS. "I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom."
DHS stated on Tuesday evening: "To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s deportation saga ends on his terms
sources.text:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s deportation saga ends on his terms
Abrego Garcia is self-deporting to Spain — after the Trump administration tried to send him to Africa.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man who was wrongly deported and then indicted by the Trump administration, has left the US on his own terms, after more than a year of legal struggles that became emblematic of the administration’s often cruel and haphazard immigration policy.
Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid, Spain, on Wednesday, after choosing to “self-deport” to a country of his choice, rather than one of the African nations to which the Trump administration was trying to send him.
It’s the conclusion — for now — of a saga that began in March 2025, when Abrego Garcia was arrested by ICE and sent to an infamous megaprison in El Salvador. (Abrego Garcia is Salvadoran and does not have US citizenship, though he’s married to a US citizen.)
At the time of his deportation, ICE was legally barred from returning him to El Salvador because of threats to his life there. Nevertheless, the Trump administration resisted returning him to the US for multiple months — and upon his return, indicted him on human smuggling charges that a judge later described as “an abuse of prosecuting power” in an opinion dismissing the charges in May 2026.
After those charges were dismissed, the administration attempted to deport Abrego García to a third country — but refused to allow him to leave for Costa Rica, which had said it would accept him. Instead, administration officials sought to send him to four different African countries to which he has no connection: Eswatini, Ghana, Liberia, and Uganda.
After failing to do so, however, it acceded last weekto Abrego Garcia’s departure to Spain, which he entered Wednesday on a temporary tourist visa.
“I am leaving with my freedom, and I am not leaving the way they removed me before, in a practically inhumane manner,” Abrego Garcia said on Wednesday after he arrived, according to CNN. “My family and I will choose the next steps.”
Trump’s ongoing deportations campaign
Abrego Garcia’s story attracted attention for being unusually tortuous, specific, and personal — but his departure doesn’t settle anything about the bigger issue, or the thousands of less well-known people in his situation.
The Trump administration hasn’t abandoned its policy of punitive deportations, often to countries with serious human rights concerns. In fact, as Wired explained on Wednesday, it’s “expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal,” including deals with 35 countries to accept US deportees and tens of thousands of deportations.
In some cases, the US is paying those countries to accept migrants — and some of those countries are so inhospitable they appear on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.
Eswatini (formerly Swaziland), where the administration attempted to send Abrego Garcia, is one of those countries. Other migrants have been sent there, according to Wired, including Pheap Rom, a Cambodian refugee who was imprisoned in Eswatini until earlier this year, when he was returned to Cambodia.
It’s a policy the Trump administration intends to continue: It’s currently asking the Supreme Court to allow it to continue removals to third countries despite the Convention Against Torture, which prevents deportations “in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” The Court will hear the case early next month, on December 9.

sources.news_title: Wrongly deported Salvadoran arrives in Spain after US legal battle
sources.text:
The Salvadoran, deported "by mistake" to a prison in El Salvador in 2025, has brought an end to 20 months of litigation in the United States, with Madrid as the first stop in what his lawyers describe as a temporary stay abroad.
Kilmar Abrego García, a Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation from the United States put him at the centre of a controversy over US President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday.
His case became a focal point in the debate over Trump's mass deportation policy in 2025, raising concerns about migrants' rights to challenge deportation orders and the administration's compliance with court rulings.
Wearing sunglasses and a baseball cap, Abrego García made his way to a vehicle at Madrid airport without speaking to reporters gathered at the scene, according to AFP journalists.
"While details remain private, Kilmar is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries," We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement.
The Salvadoran ultimately left the United States voluntarily on a commercial flight bound for Spain.
"I am leaving happy, I am leaving with my freedom," he said in a statement released by We Are CASA.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed his departure from the country in a statement, in which it labelled Abrego García a "trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator."
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, quoted in the statement.
His lawyers, for their part, welcomed the fact that their client had been able to leave "on his own terms" after his long-running dispute with the US immigration authorities.
One of his legal representatives, Simón Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the departure brought an end to a deportation campaign he described as "retaliation". He also stressed that the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego García, who is married to a US citizen, hopes to return to the United States once Donald Trump leaves the White House.
Deported "by mistake" to Bukele's mega-prison
His case began in March 2025, when federal agents arrested Abrego García in the street. Days later he was deported to El Salvador and sent to the Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), a controversial maximum-security mega-prison built on the orders of President Nayib Bukele and intended to house alleged members of criminal gangs.
The deportation went ahead even though there was a court order expressly prohibiting his deportation to El Salvador, where he had received threats from armed groups before leaving the country. The US government itself later acknowledged that it had been "a mistake", although it initially resisted facilitating his return.
Back in the United States, Abrego García reported having suffered beatings, sleep deprivation and psychological torture during the almost three months he was held in CECOT.
The legal battle reached the US Supreme Court, which ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. The authorities eventually brought him back to the country, although they did so in the context of a criminal investigation that led to an indictment over his alleged involvement in a migrant-smuggling network.
However, a federal judge ultimately dismissed all the charges, ruling that the indictment was in fact motivated by a desire to retaliate against the Salvadoran for having opposed his deportation.
The Trump administration tried to deport him to Africa
As the criminal case progressed, the US government continued trying to deport him from the country. The authorities considered sending him to Uganda, Ghana and Eswatini, but failed to secure agreement from those countries to receive him. Meanwhile, Abrego García applied for asylum to prevent his deportation.
The dispute became one of the most high-profile cases under Trump's immigration policy and highlighted the differences between the executive and judicial branches over the limits of presidential powers regarding deportations.
Throughout the process, the US president and several members of his administration publicly accused the Salvadoran of belonging to Mara Salvatrucha, also known as MS-13, as well as of human trafficking and assaulting his wife, all allegations that were echoed in the statement published on Tuesday by the DHS announcing his departure from the country.
However, these accusations were called into question by the courts. In fact, federal judge Paula Xinis, who oversaw part of the litigation in Maryland, went so far as to open a contempt-of-court inquiry against some of the prosecutors involved in the case for allegedly repeatedly disobeying her orders.
Now, with Madrid as his first stop, Abrego García plans to travel to other countries to take part in various events and speak about his experience, according to Sandoval-Moshenberg.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrives in Spain to start a new life
sources.text:
“Thank God,” Abrego said as he walked into the passport line, overwhelmed.
His wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, had not taken her eyes off the car as the police took away her husband, just as she watched Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrest him last year.
He was deported to a notorious prison in his native El Salvador, then brought back to the US, only to be charged with crimes and threatened with deportation to a country in Africa, where he had never been.
The ordeal often left Vasquez, a US citizen, in tears, and turned her into one of his most outspoken advocates.
“She’s a fighter,” Abrego said in Spanish on Wednesday (local time), as Vasquez smiled and blushed.
Like any Salvadoran citizen, Abrego is allowed to enter Spain on a valid passport and stay for up to 90 days, officials said. Abrego did not strike any agreement with the Spanish Government before arriving, one of his attorneys told reporters on Wednesday morning.
Abrego has multiple legal options available to him, said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, the attorney who accompanied him on the trip along with Vasquez, immigration advocates and Abrego’s brother Cesar. He could seek asylum in Spain or another country but has no immediate plans to do so, Sandoval Moshenberg said. He is considering speaking engagements and has connections with non-profit organisations.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said he hoped that Abrego’s stay outside the US would be short term and that he could return under a future president through his wife and son, who is also a US citizen.
Vasquez has sponsored him for legal US residency, which would put him on a path to citizenship. But under federal law, Abrego cannot return for 10 years because of the length of time he lived in the US without legal status.
His attorneys do not expect the Government to waive that penalty while Trump is in office. Another administration might, especially because of his wife and child, his attorneys said.
“You know what? He’s going to outlast this administration,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to last a lot longer than Donald Trump. And he will be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident under the next administration.”
The 31-year-old sheet metal worker, who fled El Salvador for the US at age 16, negotiated a secret settlement with the Trump Administration to quietly leave the US, according to a court order unsealed on Wednesday.
He landed in Spain in the middle of a high-stakes national election campaign in which Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has leaned heavily into his image as Europe’s leading foil to Trump.
The Spanish leader’s star has risen among the global left as he has criticised Washington’s tactics on immigration, rebuked the US war against Iran and opposed Trump’s military spending demands.
Still, Sanchez is fighting for political survival in a Sunday election dominated by affordability concerns. A loss would end his eight-year tenure and oust one of the last left-leaning governments in Europe.
Abrego was swarmed by the media as he departed the airport, but he declined an interview. A few hours after his arrival he spoke at an online news conference and thanked those who aided him, such as community organisers and Senator Christopher Van Hollen (D-Maryland) who travelled to El Salvador last year to call attention to Abrego’s detention.
Abrego emphasised at the news conference that he had “many options for my future”.
“Me and my family will choose our next steps,” he said in Spanish.
The Trump administration illegally deported Abrego to El Salvador in 2025, violating a six-year-old court order, and brought him back after courts ordered it to do so.
The Justice Department then tried to prosecute him for smuggling charges, which were tossed in court, and fought to deport him to an ever-changing series of nations in Africa.
The government has now given up that fight by allowing him to depart as a free man for a country he chose. Officials said he self-deported and paid for his own trip.
After Abrego’s flight took off, Trump officials took to social media to disparage him and bid him “good riddance”. The Department of Homeland Security said Abrego would “never” return to the US, but Sandoval-Moshenberg scoffed at that rhetoric. He said they had heard such words before.
Abrego said that he was happy. He had won his quest to leave on his own terms.
But he had also lost.
Since Trump returned to the White House, Abrego spent more than 270 days in US and Salvadoran jails, and months under house arrest in Maryland, where he had lived and worked for years before ICE detained him.
As his criminal and immigration cases were pending, he wore GPS tracking devices around each ankle.
Ultimately he had to abandon his life in the United States, a nation where he sought refuge as a teenager and hoped to stay.
Weeks after Trump returned to office in 2025, the administration deported Abrego and 260 other immigrants to El Salvador’s notorious megaprison, the Terrorism Confinement Centre, or Cecot. It was a secret operation, allegedly to expel gang members.
Many of the deportees, including Abrego, denied gang membership and had never been charged with any crime.
Those removed from the US included scores of Venezuelans who were taken to Cecot despite attempts by a federal judge to bar their removal. They, too, were eventually freed from the prison.
But Abrego’s deportation was a case apart.
Judges found that federal officials violated a 2019 court order issued during Trump’s first term that barred officials from sending him to El Salvador because as a teen he’d escaped death threats from the Barrio 18 gang in that country.
Trump officials said last year that Abrego would never return to the US, but officials brought him back after multiple courts - including the Supreme Court - ordered them to facilitate his return.
Before he left El Salvador, federal investigators reopened a previously shuttered human smuggling investigation in Tennessee, charging him with two counts that were soon thrown out by a judge.
Abrego outlasted Trump officials such as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem, who called him a “monster”, and former Attorney General Pam Bondi, who vowed that he would never return to the US. Both were ousted from their jobs in the Trump administration.
For months, Abrego had asked to go to Costa Rica, a Central American country widely regarded as safe. But he recently became concerned that the new government could force him to return to El Salvador, Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
Before Costa Rica’s presidential elections earlier this year, the government told the Washington Post the country would accept Abrego. But officials with the new administration said in October that they did not have a request pending to accept him and would have to re-evaluate the possibility if a request materialised.
Instead, Abrego set his sights on Spain.
That almost certainly will mean a prolonged separation from his wife. She has two children from a prior relationship, ages 11 and 12, and a 6-year-old son with Abrego. The oldest suffers from epilepsy and seizures, and the other two have autism. The youngest is nonverbal. All are US citizens.
US District Judge Paula Xinis in Maryland, who presided over a pair of civil lawsuits seeking Abrego’s return from El Salvador and then his release from ICE detention, issued a sealed order on Friday in the case.
The order was unsealed on Wednesday. It details terms agreed to by Abrego’s lawyers and the Justice Department for him to leave the US, and how the departure should be carried out.
She directed Abrego to depart on Tuesday. She ordered immigration authorities to remove his GPS tracking device and let him leave “unimpeded”, without being detained or diverted to another country.
Xinis said the Trump administration, after insisting for months that he be sent to a nation in Africa, notified the court that Abrego, “if he so chooses … may effectuate his own removal to any country that is willing to accept him”.
She wrote that his departure effectively executed his deportation order and said officials “shall record it as such”.
The judge ordered Abrego’s attorney to email the court by noon on Wednesday to confirm that he had left.
A Justice Department spokesperson disputed that Abrego’s voluntary departure was the result of any agreement between the parties and described it instead as an outcome ordered by the judge.
However, the spokesperson did not explain why the department did not appeal Xinis’ order.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said he was prohibited from discussing the contents of confidential settlement discussions, but he pointed out that after Xinis posted her order on Friday afternoon, the Justice Department took no steps to appeal it or seek a stay.
Instead, officials removed Abrego’s GPS tracker, screened him through security and let him go.

sources.news_title: Abrego Garcia Can ‘Breathe Freely’ After He Arrives in Spain
sources.text:
(Bloomberg) -- Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador in what US officials called an “administrative error,” said he “can breathe freely” after arriving to Spain.
“Today we celebrate because I not only feel victorious and we won the fight,” Abrego Garcia said at press conference Wednesday. “This time because I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”
Abrego Garcia’s battle was one of several high-profile legal disputes over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. He was mistakenly deported last year to CECOT, a notorious Salvadoran mega-prison, only to be brought back to face criminal charges after the US Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return to the US.
He arrived in Madrid Wednesday after the 18-month legal battle where the government had sought to deport him to African countries, including Liberia. He had also faced a US human smuggling prosecution until a US judge in May dismissed the charges, concluding the government brought the case in retaliation for his fight against deportation.
“We are going to continue to fight for all the people that are experiencing an injustice,” Abrego Garcia said. “Clearly the government did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide where my story goes from here.”
In 2019, an immigration court issued an order prohibiting the government from removing him to El Salvador after the court found he faced danger from a gang that had targeted his family.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, his American attorney, said Wednesday that Abrego Garcia traveled to Spain under a tourist visa for a “short term” stay. The US government was required by court order to lift “all impediments” that barred Abrego Garcia from leaving the country, including removing him from a no-fly list.
Abrego Garcia, whose wife and son are American citizens, could be eligible to return to the US as a legal permanent resident. But, he will need waivers from the State Department, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio will not grant, Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
“It is going to be up to the next administration to reunite this family as quickly as possible,” he said.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland who met with Abrego Garcia in the Salvadoran prison last year, said the Trump administration had engaged in a “vendetta” against him.
“Kilmar and his family are relieved that he is now in a place of his choosing, a free man and living with dignity,” Van Hollen said. “I think the message for all of us is that it’s never wrong to stand up for our Constitution. It’s never wrong to stand up for the rule of law.”
Both immigration advocates and the Trump administration said that Abrego Garcia’s departure was a win.
Ama Frimpong, chief of services and legal advocacy at We Are CASA, said rather than being deported, Abrego Garcia made the “choice” in where he went.
“This is what we fight form the freedom to choose how we live with safety and dignity,” she said.
Meanwhile, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued a statement taking credit for Abrego Garcia’s exit. He labeled Abrego Garcia as a “human trafficker” and “MS-13 gang member.”
Abrego Garcia has denied the government’s allegations.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Leaves America After Fierce Deportation Battle — So What Was He Really Fighting For?
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant whose wrongful deportation to a notorious prison triggered a national political firestorm, has voluntarily left the United States for Spain, bringing a remarkable new chapter to one of the most contentious immigration cases of President Donald Trump’s second administration.
The departure, confirmed by federal officials and Abrego Garcia’s attorneys on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, comes after nearly 20 months of legal confrontations involving federal judges, the Supreme Court, congressional lawmakers and the Trump administration.
But the announcement has also prompted a question that may resonate with Americans who followed his case: If Abrego Garcia was ultimately willing to leave the country, why did he fight deportation so aggressively in the first place?
The apparent contradiction is politically compelling, but the legal answer is considerably more complicated.
Abrego Garcia’s legal battle was never simply about securing an unconditional right to remain in the United States. It also concerned the government’s decision to send him to a country where a judge had already determined he faced persecution, the administration’s efforts to deport him to other countries, and the legal protections available to people facing removal.
His departure to Spain does not erase those disputes. Instead, it raises new questions about whether the outcome represents a victory for the Trump administration, a vindication of Abrego Garcia’s legal arguments or a compromise that allowed both sides to claim success.
Trump Administration Celebrates as Abrego Garcia Leaves for Spain
The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that Abrego Garcia departed the United States on Tuesday aboard a commercial flight bound for Madrid.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin welcomed the announcement.
“We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” Mullin wrote on X.
The administration characterized his departure as another success in its immigration enforcement campaign.
According to the Associated Press, DHS said Abrego Garcia received no incentives to leave and would not be permitted to return to the United States.
But his attorneys offered a sharply different interpretation.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of Abrego Garcia’s lawyers, said his client had spent much of the previous year and a half seeking permission to leave the country on terms that would protect his freedom.
Rather than being forcibly transported to Liberia in federal custody, Abrego Garcia was permitted to board a commercial flight to Spain.
His attorney described the outcome as a negotiated departure that allowed him to travel freely.
Abrego Garcia himself expressed relief.
“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom,” he said in a statement reported by the Associated Press.
For supporters of the administration’s immigration policies, however, the central fact remains that Abrego Garcia is no longer in the United States.
For his lawyers, the crucial distinction is that he left for a country of his choosing rather than being sent involuntarily to a destination selected by the government.
Why Did He Fight So Hard if He Was Willing to Leave?
The answer begins with an immigration court ruling from 2019.
Abrego Garcia entered the United States without authorization as a teenager and later settled in Maryland, where he established a family.
In 2019, an immigration judge determined that he faced a credible threat of persecution if returned to El Salvador.
The judge granted him a protection known as withholding of removal.
That ruling did not make Abrego Garcia a permanent legal resident or provide him with a pathway to citizenship.
However, it prohibited the federal government from deporting him to El Salvador while the protection remained in effect.
He was permitted to remain in the United States and work under immigration supervision.
In March 2025, federal authorities nevertheless arrested him and transferred him to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, commonly known as CECOT.
The Justice Department subsequently acknowledged that his removal had resulted from an administrative error. The distinction matters.
Abrego Garcia’s legal challenge was not based on a claim that immigration law prevented the United States from ever deporting him.
Rather, the government had sent him to a specific country despite an existing judicial order prohibiting that action.
His attorneys argued that the administration was required to respect the court’s ruling and provide the legal process necessary to determine what could happen next.
In April 2025, the Supreme Court upheld an order requiring the administration to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody and ensure his case proceeded as though the improper deportation had not occurred.
That was a significant legal development independent of whether Abrego Garcia would eventually remain in America.
Legal Experts Explain Why Due Process Matters
The controversy surrounding Abrego Garcia became part of a broader debate about presidential authority and the constitutional protections afforded to noncitizens.
Amy Grenier, an attorney with the American Immigration Lawyers Association, emphasized that the Constitution does not restrict due-process protections exclusively to American citizens.
“The thing about due process is that it either applies to everyone present in the United States or it applies to no one,” Grenier told FactCheck.org in April 2025.
Her observation addresses the central legal issue behind Abrego Garcia’s case.
People who enter the country unlawfully can still be subject to deportation. But the government must follow applicable legal procedures, including complying with court orders that limit where an individual may be removed.
Matthew Waxman, a senior fellow specializing in law and foreign policy at the Council on Foreign Relations, addressed the separation-of-powers implications in an April 2025 analysis.
“But courts are not barred altogether from enforcing the law in such matters,” Waxman explained.
He also warned that aggressive assertions of executive authority could provoke greater judicial involvement in immigration and foreign-policy disputes.
Northwestern University law professor Monica Haymond raised a related concern about the practical limits of judicial authority.
In comments published in April 2025, she observed that courts can consider sanctions against officials or agencies that fail to comply with their orders, although such measures can encounter institutional obstacles.
Together, those legal assessments suggest that Abrego Garcia’s case involved issues extending well beyond one individual’s immigration status.
The broader question was whether the executive branch could disregard judicial restrictions when carrying out its deportation policies.
A Second Deportation Fight Made the Situation Even More Complicated
After the administration returned Abrego Garcia to the United States in June 2025, his legal troubles continued.
Federal prosecutors charged him with human smuggling in Tennessee, stemming from an earlier traffic stop.
Abrego Garcia denied the allegations, and his attorneys argued that the prosecution was retaliation for his successful challenge to the government’s deportation actions.
In May 2026, a federal judge dismissed the criminal case, finding that the prosecution was improperly motivated. The government appealed that decision.
Meanwhile, immigration officials continued exploring options to remove Abrego Garcia from the United States.
Among the proposed destinations were Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued that if he were required to leave the country, he should be allowed to relocate to Costa Rica, which had agreed to receive him.
The Trump administration resisted that proposal.
According to the Associated Press, former acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director Todd Lyons argued in a March 2026 memorandum that sending Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be prejudicial to American interests, given the resources expended on arrangements with Liberia.
The dispute over his destination became a major obstacle to resolving the case.
In other words, the administration and Abrego Garcia were not simply arguing over whether he would remain in the United States.
They were also fighting over where he could be sent, the circumstances of his departure and whether his legal rights would be respected.
His eventual relocation to Spain offers a clearer explanation for his previous resistance.
The Immigration Fight Creates Two Competing Political Narratives
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused Abrego Garcia of membership in the MS-13 gang, allegations he denies.
Administration officials have also cited criminal allegations and domestic abuse accusations in explaining why they considered his removal necessary.
Those accusations have been politically significant, but they must be distinguished from the question of whether the government was legally permitted to deport him to El Salvador in violation of the 2019 order.
Critics of the administration argue that a person’s immigration status or alleged misconduct does not eliminate the government’s responsibility to obey the law.
Supporters of tougher immigration enforcement counter that Abrego Garcia entered the country unlawfully and that his ultimate departure demonstrates the administration’s ability to enforce removal orders.
Both sides can point to elements of the outcome supporting their arguments.
Trump officials secured the departure of a man whose continued presence they had strongly opposed.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys secured his release from the threat of forced transfer to Liberia and arranged travel to Spain.
Neither accomplishment, however, settles every legal question raised by the case.
Could Abrego Garcia Eventually Return to America?
Another important aspect of Tuesday’s announcement concerns whether Abrego Garcia’s departure is necessarily permanent. His lawyers do not believe that it must be.
Sandoval-Moshenberg suggested that his client could seek to return to the United States under a future administration more willing to reconsider his circumstances.
DHS, however, maintains that he will not be allowed back into the country.
That disagreement is significant because Abrego Garcia’s wife and children remain in the United States.
His departure therefore creates the prospect of an extended family separation, even though the legal fight over his treatment has attracted national attention.
Whether he eventually obtains permission to return will depend on immigration law, the terms of his departure and decisions by future federal authorities.
There is no guarantee that a change of administration would automatically make him eligible for readmission.
The Real Meaning of Abrego Garcia’s Departure
The question circulating on social media — why fight so hard to stay in America only to leave voluntarily? — is understandable.
But it assumes that the objective of every immigration appeal is permanent residence. That is not always the case.
A person facing deportation may contest the government’s authority to send them to a particular country, challenge the procedures used to remove them, seek release from detention or attempt to negotiate a departure to a safer destination.
Abrego Garcia’s case involved several of those issues.
His departure to Spain illustrates that fighting deportation and ultimately leaving the United States are not necessarily contradictory actions.
It also illustrates the competing priorities that have driven the controversy.
For the Trump administration, removing Abrego Garcia from American territory represents the desired immigration enforcement outcome.
For his lawyers, obtaining his freedom and the ability to choose his destination represents a meaningful result after months of litigation.
For the courts, the case has raised questions about the government’s obligation to respect judicial decisions.
And for the American public, it offers an opportunity to distinguish between whether someone has a legal right to remain in the country and whether the government has a legal right to remove that person in a particular manner.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia may have left the United States, but his departure does not establish that his legal fight was pointless. It shows that the fight was about much more than simply staying in America.

sources.text:
Trump DHS Chief Markwayne Mullin's Abrego Garcia Victory Lap Draws Rebuke From Former GOP Senate Counsel — as He Point to Failed Liberia Deportation Bid: 'Shameful and Dishonest'
Nov. 25 2026, Published 1:06 p.m. ET
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing criticism over his response to Kilmar Abrego Garcia's departure for Spain, with a former Republican Senate counsel accusing him of misrepresenting the outcome of the high-profile immigration case. RadarOnline.com reports.
Abrego Garcia left the United States on Tuesday, November 24, aboard a commercial flight under an agreement with the Trump administration, according to his legal team. His departure followed months of legal battles over the government's efforts to deport him to countries he did not want to go to.
The Department of Homeland Security described the move as a "self-deportation" in a social media post. The agency said Mullin was "delighted" by the development and declared that Abrego Garcia would "never be allowed back inside the United States."
DHS also said he departed under a removal order and paid for his own flight. However, critics questioned whether the administration's description accurately reflected how the agreement came about.
Former GOP Senate Counsel Calls Mullin's Statement 'Shameful and Dishonest'
Gregg Nunziata, a former chief nominations counsel for Senate Judiciary Republicans who now heads the conservative Society for the Rule of Law, publicly challenged Mullin's characterization of the departure.
"I suppose it's only fitting that this entire disgraceful, lawless story would end with a shameful and dishonest post from our DHS Secretary," Nunziata wrote on X.
Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, also accused the administration of trying to put a favorable spin on the outcome.
He pointed to the government's unsuccessful effort to send Abrego Garcia to Liberia, despite Costa Rica's willingness to accept him. Reichlin-Melnick also noted that Abrego Garcia had previously agreed to leave for Costa Rica in August 2025, but the administration rejected that arrangement.
Abrego Garcia's attorneys maintained that their client ultimately left voluntarily and on his own terms. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described him as "a free man" and said the departure was temporary, with potential options for returning to the United States.
Administration's Push to Deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia Failed
The dispute over Abrego Garcia's destination became a major obstacle for the administration. Officials had pursued his removal to several African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Liberia, despite his objections.
Abrego Garcia had offered to leave for Costa Rica instead. According to his attorneys, the Central American country was willing to grant him refugee status, but the administration opposed the arrangement and continued pursuing Liberia.
The effort to send him to Liberia was ultimately blocked in court. The administration's position also faced scrutiny after a March 2026 memo from former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons argued that sending Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States.
Abrego Garcia's Mistaken Deportation Sparked a Lengthy Court Battle
The controversy dates back to March 2025, when federal agents deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador despite a 2019 immigration court order protecting him from removal to his home country because of threats from a gang.
He was sent to the country's notorious CECOT prison. The government subsequently acknowledged that his deportation was an administrative error.
Following a Supreme Court order directing the administration to facilitate his return, Abrego Garcia came back to the United States in June 2025. Prosecutors then charged him with human smuggling, allegations he denied.
In May 2026, a federal judge dismissed the criminal case, finding that the prosecution had been pursued with a vindictive motive. The Justice Department appealed the decision.
Chris Van Hollen Celebrates Abrego Garcia's Departure
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador to advocate for Abrego Garcia's release, welcomed his departure and described it as a victory for due process.
"Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity," Van Hollen said in a November 24 statement.
Abrego Garcia's attorneys have emphasized that Spain is not necessarily his permanent destination. His lawyer told NPR that he intends to decide where to settle over the next two years and believes he has options to return to the United States.
The Salvadoran national also has an American wife and child in Maryland, and his legal team has expressed hope that a future administration could help reunite the family.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the “Maryland father” who was really a Salvadoran illegal alien and has been accused of being a “human smuggler, wife beater, gang member, and child predator,” self-deported to Spain on Tuesday following removal orders from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). But Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who jet-set to San Salvador to conduct a welfare check during Garcia’s first deportation, is just “relieved” he will finally be a “free man.”
“Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity,” Van Hollen said. “While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”
The Maryland Democrat’s initial trip to San Salvador in 2025 was for the express purpose to “bring him home,” even though he was already back in his home country. Van Hollen’s purpose was different, as my colleague Eddie Scarry wrote: “the senator [was] attempting to re-import an illegal alien who was lawfully removed from the country.”
Van Hollen, who is currently challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the top Senate leadership position in the upcoming Congress, is once again expressing more interest in the well-being of an illegal alien who has been accused of multiple crimes than the American people.
To Van Hollen, it was all about “uphold[ing] his constitutional rights.”
At least the much-beleaguered Garcia “will be safe” outside the United States, Van Hollen said.
“Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. DHS stated that Garcia paid his own way out of the country and did not receive any taxpayer dollars that have been offered to others to self-deport.
Garcia was a “known member” of MS-13, a notoriously violent gang that has been designated a foreign terrorist organization. According to DHS, he was in possession of drugs and rolls of money during his arrest and was arrested alongside two other gang members.
He was also pulled over on a highway transporting eight passengers with no luggage, for which DHS accused him of human trafficking. Garcia is also accused of being a child predator, as court documents allege he “solicited nude photographs and videos of a minor.”
Garcia has been accused of domestic violence numerous times, with his wife filing petitions with a court against him. “She alleged that Garcia verbally abused her, kicked her, slapped her, shoved her, mentally abused her kids, locking them in their bedroom while they cried, and detained Vasquez against her will. In the 2021 filing, Vasquez claimed he bruised, punched, and scratched her while ripping off her shirt,” DHS stated.
But as Van Hollen said, Garcia obtaining his “freedom” and “dignity” is a “good day for Kilmar Abrego Garcia and his family.”

sources.news_title: Quiet Deportation to Spain Ends Abrego Garcia Saga
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has arrived in Madrid after the Trump administration finally acceded to his request to be deported to Spain, a country agreeable to him — which is what federal immigration law calls for when such an accommodation is practicable.
Thus ends, for now, a nearly two-year saga that we’ve covered extensively (see, e.g., here). We have to qualify with “for now” because, after all the twists and turns, there’s a very good chance that Abrego (whose wife and child are American citizens) will be triumphantly readmitted to the United States — this time, lawfully — if a Democrat is elected president in 2028. For immigration hawks (such as moi), his case is a cautionary tale in how benighted execution of a popular enforcement policy can turn a political asset into a liability.

sources.text:
Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.
The move ends 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents in March 2025 and erroneously deported to his native country.
Neither his attorneys nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday from States Newsroom.
But in a statement released shortly after midnight Wednesday morning, the immigration advocacy group We Are CASA said Abrego Garcia had “cleared his name of the Trump administration’s bogus charges against him and walked out of the United States a free man.”
The statement said Abrego Garcia was accompanied on a commercial flight by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney and a We Are CASA representative. It said they were met at the airport by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who removed the ankle monitoring bracelet Abrego Garcia has had to wear since courts ordered him released from detention and returned home to Beltsville.
Abrego Garcia said in the statement that “justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”
“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom. I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight,” his statement said. “I feel good. I feel confident. I believe everything will be okay because God is with us.”
Abrego Garcia’s deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.
Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.
It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S. and said he was “relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution.”
“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
Neither Van Hollen nor We Are CASA specified Abrego Garcia’s destination, but news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.
The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Uganda, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.
A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there. But it did not prevent the government from trying to send him to a third country — an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.
Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.
“Mr. Abrego Garcia had been asking permission to leave the country since August 2025,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of his attorneys, in the We Are CASA statement. “The Trump Administration held him and refused to allow him to depart, first in an ICE detention center for five months and then on electronic monitoring in Maryland for almost a year, all the while insisting on deporting him to a series of African countries. That retaliatory deportation campaign has now come to an end.”
Abrego Garcia was eventually returned from El Salvador in June 2025, but was immediately arrested and charged by ICE with human smuggling in Tennessee. Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding in Tennessee, when Abrego was driving an SUV carrying a number of Latino men.
Abrego Garcia was let go with a warning after the traffic stop and the case was closed. But federal officials reopened it two years later and charged Abrego Garcia with human smuggling as soon as he was returned from El Salvador.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued the flimsy charges were mere pretext to punish their client after he beat the administration in court. A federal judge in Tennessee agreed in May and tossed the case out as a vindictive prosecution and an abuse of government power.
It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen’s statement said.
Ama Frimpong, We Are CASA’s chief of legal services and another of Abrego Garcia’s attoenrys, called it “a victory that Kilmar gets to choose what comes next.”
“He is choosing where and how to lead his life. He is beginning this new chapter with the safety, freedom, and dignity he fought to reclaim,” Frimpong said in the statement. “That victory belongs first to Kilmar; to Jennifer, whose voice carried their family’s fight across the country; and to their family, who endured more than any family should.

sources.news_title: To Get Justice, Kilmar Abrego Garcia Had to Leave Trump’s America
sources.text:
In the end, Kilmar Ábrego García’s extraordinary 20-month struggle against Donald Trump’s crazed persecution and vilification campaign against him concluded with a single, quiet gesture. As Ábrego García stood in Dulles Airport, a federal agent unlocked and removed his ankle bracelet.
“Thank you,” Ábrego García said to the man who removed his last remaining shackle, which he’d been wearing for nearly a year. And that was the end of that.
Ábrego García is now a free man. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, confirmed to me that the government dropped its effort to remove him to a country of its choosing—leaving him free to go anywhere outside the United States he desires—provided he do so by November 24. He boarded a flight to Spain, where he landed Wednesday morning and will enter on a tourist’s visa.
We obtained video of Ábrego García’s final unshackling. It’s a surprisingly anticlimactic moment, given that it brings to an end perhaps the most deranged vendetta ever waged by an American president against a single individual.
Ábrego García succeeded in securing a measure of justice—and managed to defeat Trump’s efforts to persecute him—even if he had to leave the United States to do so.
That’s not how Trump’s propagandists are spinning this outcome, of course. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pretended it was a victory for Trump, claiming that “we are delighted” that Ábrego García has “self-deported from the United States to Spain.”
Because there is no limit to Mullin’s bootlicking self-debasement on Trump’s behalf, his statement repeated a barrage of slander about Ábrego García that the government could never make stick despite well over a year of efforts to make it so.
But Mullin’s display of exultation is hollow. Make no mistake: Trump, Mullin, and Stephen Miller—the architect of the campaign against Ábrego García—absolutely did not get their way with regard to Ábrego García’s fate.
At no point in this saga did Trump and Miller secure the maximum subjugation and humiliation for Ábrego García they craved. Let’s roll the tape: First, Trump’s deportation forces removed him in March 2025 to a gulag in El Salvador, violating a 2019 court order that had resolved the Salvadoran’s undocumented status by prohibiting his removal to that particular country.
When the administration acknowledged this had been done in “error,” Miller rushed to declare that it wasn’t an error at all. Why? Because Miller badly wanted this case to set an example demonstrating Trump’s power to decree undesirables subject to removal by dictatorial fiat, outside due process and the law.
That failed. The Supreme Court ordered Trump to facilitate Ábrego García’s return, which the administration ultimately did. Trump and his top agency heads then unleashed months of state propaganda depicting him as an MS-13 member and worse, all to make it true that he was a criminal who deserved imprisonment or exile.
Yet despite deploying the entire federal government to try to find evidence of this, Trump and Miller never could do so—that smear campaign, too, failed. Federal prosecutors then brought criminal charges against Ábrego García for allegedly trafficking migrants—a case so questionable that one veteran prosecutor resigned. As Politico’s Josh Gerstein and Kyle Cheney detail, it’s been so dubious all along that a judge temporarily tossed it due to its plainly vindictive nature.
It’s crucial to recall that throughout Ábrego García’s prosecution, the government sought to remove him to various African countries, which declined to take him. Incredibly, even though he’d agreed to be deported to Costa Rica, the government refused to send him there, apparently because it couldn’t be spun as a glorious triumph for Trump.
So let’s be clear: This effort also failed. Trump and Miller wanted Ábrego García either imprisoned in the United States or deported to a place of their choosing, one that inflicted maximal degradation for the crime of embarrassing the Despot. Neither outcome happened.
Indeed, because the government couldn’t successfully deport him on Trump’s terms, it finally agreed to let Ábrego García decamp to a country of his choosing. “Instead of being shackled on an ICE Air flight to Africa, he left on a United Airlines economy-plus flight to a destination he selected,” attorney Sandoval-Moshenberg told me.
What’s really been at stake all throughout is whether Trump and Miller could simply suspend the rule of law to exert their preferred punishment on a designated enemy of the state. Illegal removal to a foreign torture prison; months of state-sponsored vilification; an obviously vindictive prosecution; the push to deport him to a country selected by Trump and only Trump—it all failed.
This is not Ábrego García’s preferred outcome. He wanted to remain in the United States with his wife and American-born children, who are all U.S. citizens. But here’s the bottom line: No matter how hard lickspittles like Mullin spin otherwise, Trump and Miller did not get their way. Ábrego García remains unbowed.
Indeed, if a Democrat becomes president in 2029, it’s easy to envision Ábrego García getting paroled back into our country. After all, in a very real sense, he’s the victim of state persecution at the hands of the United States. If he had to leave Trump’s America to get the justice due to him, the next president can bring him back and complete the circle.
“He’s got a clear path back to the United States under the next administration, by virtue of his U.S. citizen wife,” Sandoval-Moshenberg told me. “Kilmar will outlast Donald Trump.”
Ábrego García is already receiving invitations to speak at universities and civil society organizations in at least four different countries, where he’ll tell his side of the story, says Chris Newman, a lawyer for his family.
“The Trump administration’s campaign to destroy Kilmar backfired massively,” Newman told me. “For over 600 days, they told the world lie after lie about Kilmar and his family. Kilmar endured.” People fighting for democracy and the rule of law in the United States and beyond, Newman added, will “now look to him for inspiration.”
Trump and Miller brought the full weight of the federal government to bear against this young day laborer and father in one of the most extraordinary abuses of power in modern U.S. history. The case may one day be taught in law schools as a sign of our brush with authoritarianism. Should he end up back in here in 2029, a free man, it ultimately may also be sanctified as a sign of our democratic resilience.

sources.news_title: Trump Finally Gets His Wish As Kilmar Ábrego García Leaves The US
sources.text:
Trump Gets His Wish As Kilmar Ábrego García Leaves The US
Trump Finally Gets His Wish As Kilmar Ábrego García Leaves The US
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Maryland immigrant at the center of an abduction and deportation by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has left the United States on his own to end a months-long battle with the Trump administration.
The Salvadoran immigrant was at the center of an unrelenting battle with the Trump administration since March 2025, when Garcia was detained and deported by ICE. He was deported back to El Salvador despite a court order allowing Garcia protection in the United States, the Guardian reports.
Garcia was ultimately returned to the U.S. after the Supreme Court found that he shouldn’t have been deported. Since his return, Garcia has been fighting with the Department of Homeland Security, which was trying to send Garcia anywhere as long as he wasn’t in the United States.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he would leave on his own and therefore would avoid being forcibly sent to an unfamiliar country.
In a statement, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who fought to bring Garcia back from El Salvador last year, called him a “free man.”
“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”
The Trump administration doesn’t care that the 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years; they are only concerned that as a teen he immigrated into the country illegally. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that Garcia couldn’t be deported back to El Salvador because he was in danger, as a gang had threatened him and his family. The judge’s decision allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under the Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was never given permanent residency status.
Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and sent to a Salvadoran prison. ICE claimed that the detainment and subsequent deportation were an “administrative error.” After pressure from the public and a court order, the Trump administration relented and brought Garcia back to America in June 2025 only after charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge found the charges to be bogus and dismissed the case in May, finding that the Justice Department was merely trying to punish Garcia for challenging his deportation.
The Trump administration then pushed to send García to a third country and even threatened to send him to places he’d never been, like Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
