sources.news_title: A timeline of key events in Kilmar Ábrego García’s fight with the Trump administration
sources.text:
By The Associated Press
Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.
In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Here is a timeline of key events:
Arrival: around 2011
Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
Arrest: March 28, 2019
Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Immigration court: Oct. 10, 2019
A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.
Detained by ICE: March 12, 2025
Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.
Deportation: March 15, 2025
Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.
Supreme Court: April 10, 2025
The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.
Senator visits: April 17, 2025
In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.
Criminal charges: June 6, 2025
Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.
Attempts at second deportation: July 23, 2025
ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.
Released from jail: Aug. 22, 2025
Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.
In immigration custody: Aug. 25, 2025
Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.
Judge orders release: Dec. 11, 2025
A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.
No immigration detention: Feb. 17, 2026
A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.
Judge dismisses criminal case: May 22, 2026
A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution.”
Prosecutors argue for reinstating criminal charges: Aug. 17, 2026
The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.
Self-deportation: Nov. 24, 2026
Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.
Arrival in Spain: Nov. 25, 2026
Ábrego García lands at Madrid’s international airport. He doesn’t speak to reporters but raises a fist as he enters a van.

sources.news_title: Abrego Garcia flies to Spain, ending 20-month deportation battle with Trump administration • Oklahoma Voice
sources.text:
Abrego Garcia flies to Spain, ending 20-month deportation battle with Trump administration
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department was ‘delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain.’
Kilmar Abrego Garcia stands outside U.S. District Court in Greenbelt in December 2025 beside his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, left, and Lydia Walther-Rodriguez with CASA, after a federal judge ruled he was allowed to remain free. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.
The move ends 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents in March 2025 and erroneously deported to his native country.
In a statement late Tuesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department was “delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” fulfilling the administration’s promise that he “would not remain in our country.”
But in a statement released shortly after midnight Wednesday morning, the immigration advocacy group We Are CASA said Abrego Garcia had “cleared his name of the Trump administration’s bogus charges against him and walked out of the United States a free man.”
The statement said Abrego Garcia was accompanied on a commercial flight by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney and a We Are CASA representative. It said they were met at the airport by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who removed the ankle monitoring bracelet Abrego Garcia has had to wear since courts ordered him released from detention and returned home to Beltsville.
Abrego Garcia said in the statement that “justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”
“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom. I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight,” his statement said. “I feel good. I feel confident. I believe everything will be okay because God is with us.”
Abrego Garcia’s deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.
Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.
It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S. and said he was “relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution.”
“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”
Neither Van Hollen nor We Are CASA specified Abrego Garcia’s destination, but news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.
The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Uganda, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.
A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there. But it did not prevent the government from trying to send him to a third country – an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.
Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.
“Mr. Abrego Garcia had been asking permission to leave the country since August 2025,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of his attorneys, in the We Are CASA statement. “The Trump Administration held him and refused to allow him to depart, first in an ICE detention center for five months and then on electronic monitoring in Maryland for almost a year, all the while insisting on deporting him to a series of African countries. That retaliatory deportation campaign has now come to an end.”
Abrego Garcia was eventually returned from El Salvador in June 2025, but was immediately arrested and charged by ICE with human smuggling in Tennessee. Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding in Tennessee, when Abrego was driving an SUV carrying a number of Latino men.
Abrego Garcia was let go with a warning after the traffic stop and the case was closed. But federal officials reopened it two years later and charged Abrego Garcia with human smuggling as soon as he was returned from El Salvador.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued the flimsy charges were mere pretext to punish their client after he beat the administration in court. A federal judge in Tennessee agreed in May and tossed the case out as a vindictive prosecution and an abuse of government power.
It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen’s statement said.
Ama Frimpong, We Are CASA’s chief of legal services and another of Abrego Garcia’s attoenrys, called it “a victory that Kilmar gets to choose what comes next.”
“He is choosing where and how to lead his life. He is beginning this new chapter with the safety, freedom, and dignity he fought to reclaim,” Frimpong said in the statement. “That victory belongs first to Kilmar; to Jennifer, whose voice carried their family’s fight across the country; and to their family, who endured more than any family should.
— This story was updated Wednesday morning to include comments from the Department of Homeland Security and We Are CASA, and details of the Tennessee charges against Abrego Garcia.
This story was originally produced by Maryland Matters, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Oklahoma Voice, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Arrives in Spain After Voluntary Departure, Ending Lengthy U.S. Deportation Battle
sources.text:
The Salvadoran national, whose mistaken deportation to El Salvador triggered a prolonged legal dispute with the Trump administration, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after agreeing to leave the United States rather than face removal to Liberia.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a 31-year-old Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally and became the subject of a high-profile immigration dispute with the Trump administration, arrived in Spain on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after voluntarily departing the United States under an agreement with federal authorities.
Abrego Garcia landed at Madrid’s Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport after traveling on a commercial flight Tuesday. His departure potentially concludes nearly 20 months of legal proceedings involving his mistaken deportation to El Salvador, subsequent return to the United States and the administration’s efforts to remove him to another country.
According to Reuters’ report from Madrid, Abrego Garcia arrived wearing sunglasses and a Chicago Bulls cap before leaving the airport in a vehicle without addressing reporters.
The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Tuesday night that he had left the United States voluntarily, describing the departure as a self-deportation carried out under an existing removal order.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin welcomed the development in a statement posted on X.
“We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” Mullin wrote.
DHS said Abrego Garcia received no financial incentives for leaving and would not be permitted to return to the United States.
His attorneys disputed the suggestion that his departure permanently resolves his immigration status, describing the move as temporary and indicating that he intends to pursue opportunities to return legally.
The Associated Press reported Wednesday that Abrego Garcia issued a statement celebrating his ability to choose his destination after months of legal uncertainty.
“The U.S. government may be the most powerful government in the world, but justice can still prevail,” he said.
“In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”
His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the arrangement allowed Abrego Garcia to leave freely rather than face removal to an African country selected by immigration authorities.
“The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world,” Sandoval-Moshenberg told NPR.
The attorney described the departure as a temporary arrangement and said Abrego Garcia could eventually seek lawful permanent residency through his family relationships.
Abrego Garcia is married to an American citizen, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, and is the father of a U.S. citizen child.
His legal team maintains that those relationships could provide a potential pathway for his eventual return, although such an outcome would require compliance with applicable immigration laws.
“We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
He indicated that Abrego Garcia would decide where to settle while awaiting the end of Trump’s presidency.
The legal dispute began in March 2025, when federal immigration authorities arrested Abrego Garcia in Maryland and deported him to El Salvador.
He was transferred to the country’s high-security Terrorism Confinement Center, commonly known as CECOT, despite a 2019 immigration court order prohibiting his removal to El Salvador because of concerns that he could face persecution.
The Trump administration subsequently acknowledged that the removal violated the existing court protection and described the incident as an administrative error.
However, administration officials initially resisted efforts to return him to the United States, arguing that his detention in El Salvador complicated the government’s ability to secure his release.
The dispute reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which directed the administration to facilitate his return and ensure that his immigration proceedings complied with federal law.
After months of litigation and diplomatic negotiations, Abrego Garcia was returned to the United States in June 2025.
Federal prosecutors subsequently charged him with offenses involving the alleged transportation of immigrants without legal authorization.
The criminal case originated from a November 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee, when law enforcement officers encountered Abrego Garcia driving a vehicle containing several passengers.
Federal prosecutors alleged that the incident was connected to an illegal immigrant transportation operation extending from Texas to Maryland.
Abrego Garcia denied the allegations, and his attorneys argued that the criminal prosecution was retaliatory because he had challenged his mistaken deportation.
A federal judge dismissed the charges in May 2026 after concluding that the government’s prosecution was improperly motivated by his legal challenge.
The dismissal removed a major obstacle to resolving his immigration proceedings but did not automatically establish his right to remain in the United States.
Separately, the Trump administration accused Abrego Garcia of having connections to the MS-13 criminal gang, an allegation he has repeatedly denied.
Government officials cited earlier law enforcement records and statements by investigators as the basis for their concerns.
The administration also publicized domestic violence allegations involving his wife.
In 2021, Vasquez Sura sought a protective order against Abrego Garcia after alleging domestic abuse. She subsequently said she had filed the request as a precaution and defended her husband following his deportation.
Those allegations did not result in a criminal conviction establishing domestic violence, and they were separate from the legal question of whether the government could deport him in violation of the 2019 order.
The combination of gang allegations, domestic violence accusations and immigration proceedings made Abrego Garcia’s case a central point of disagreement between supporters and critics of Trump’s immigration enforcement policies.
Administration officials argued that his immigration status and alleged criminal associations justified removal from the country.
His attorneys and supporters maintained that the government was required to follow court orders and provide lawful procedures regardless of his immigration status or accusations against him.
Following his return from El Salvador, the administration sought to deport him to several countries other than his homeland.
Those proposals included countries in Africa where Abrego Garcia had no established personal connections.
The government’s efforts eventually focused on Liberia, prompting another round of legal challenges.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued that he should be allowed to relocate voluntarily to a country willing to accept him rather than be transported involuntarily to Liberia.
His legal team previously identified Costa Rica as a potential destination, saying the country’s authorities were willing to provide him with protection.
However, the administration did not approve that arrangement.
According to ABC News’ account of the negotiations, the dispute continued for months as lawyers negotiated possible destinations and legal conditions governing his departure.
The case eventually shifted toward permitting Abrego Garcia to arrange his own travel.
A federal judge allowed him to leave by a specified deadline, avoiding the prospect of another forced removal while ending his immediate physical presence in the United States.
The decision to travel to Spain emerged after negotiations between his legal representatives and federal authorities.
There was no immediate indication that Abrego Garcia entered Spain under a special agreement with Spanish immigration officials.
His precise immigration status in Spain remained unclear Wednesday.
The departure also drew a response from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who had traveled to El Salvador in April 2025 to meet Abrego Garcia while he was detained.
Van Hollen welcomed the agreement allowing him to travel independently.
The senator said Abrego Garcia was departing for a country of his choosing as a free man, rather than remaining subject to detention while immigration authorities pursued removal to another destination.
The outcome carries different implications for the administration and Abrego Garcia’s legal team.
For the Trump administration, his departure satisfies the immediate objective of removing a foreign national who lacked legal authorization to remain in the United States.
For his attorneys, the arrangement avoids another forced deportation and preserves the possibility of pursuing future legal immigration options.
The agreement does not erase the earlier finding that Abrego Garcia was improperly deported to El Salvador in 2025.
Nor does his voluntary departure establish the truth of the criminal allegations previously raised against him.
The case also illustrates the distinction between a federal government’s authority to remove an individual without lawful immigration status and the legal restrictions governing where and how that removal may occur.
Immigration courts can prohibit deportation to a particular country when an individual establishes that returning there would expose them to qualifying risks of persecution or torture.
Such protection does not necessarily provide lawful permanent residency or prevent removal to another country legally authorized to accept the individual.
Abrego Garcia’s original protection concerned deportation to El Salvador, leaving the administration able to pursue other destinations within the limits imposed by immigration law and court orders.
His voluntary relocation to Spain represents a negotiated resolution of that immediate dispute.
However, questions remain about whether he will obtain long-term residency in Spain, relocate elsewhere or eventually seek permission to return to his family in Maryland.
DHS has stated that he will not be allowed back into the United States, while his attorneys maintain that future legal options remain available.
Those positions reflect an unresolved disagreement about his potential immigration prospects rather than an announced decision granting or denying a future application.
With his arrival in Madrid confirmed Wednesday, Abrego Garcia is no longer in U.S. immigration custody and has left the country voluntarily.
The development brings a significant phase of the prolonged deportation dispute to an end while leaving open questions about his permanent destination and the possibility of eventual family reunification in the United States.

sources.news_title: Abrego Garcia Leaves US for Spain, Ending Long Fight
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man whose mistaken deportation to a notorious prison in El Salvador became one of the defining cases of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, has left the United States voluntarily for Spain, ending a legal fight that stretched across nearly two years.
Abrego Garcia boarded a flight from Washington Dulles International Airport to Madrid on Tuesday and arrived in the Spanish capital on Wednesday, according to his attorneys and federal officials. Video recorded at Dulles showed him walking through the airport with his wife and several supporters, including an advocate from the immigrant rights group CASA. Before passing through security, he went to a U.S. Customs and Border Protection office, where an ankle monitor he had been required to wear was to be removed, according to a person familiar with the arrangement.
"I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom," Abrego Garcia said in a statement. He said he was departing "with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me."
The departure was the product of a negotiated agreement between his lawyers and government attorneys, and its terms remain sealed. A person familiar with the case said a judge had told Abrego Garcia to self-deport by Tuesday. Sealed filings were entered in his federal case in Maryland last week.
Both sides moved quickly to claim the outcome as a win.
The Department of Homeland Security said Abrego Garcia "self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order," that he received no incentives to leave and that he will not be allowed back into the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on social media that he was "delighted" by the departure and repeated the administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia was a member of the MS-13 gang, a claim Abrego Garcia has consistently denied.
His lawyers offered a very different reading. Attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg called it a temporary departure while his client "waits out the end of this administration." He said Abrego Garcia has options to return to the United States because he is married to a U.S. citizen, but acknowledged, "We don't expect that to happen under this administration." He said he expects "the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland." Another attorney, Sean Hecker, confirmed that Spain was his client's destination.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to El Salvador last year to meet Abrego Garcia in custody and became one of his most prominent advocates, welcomed the news. "I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free," Van Hollen said.
It was not immediately clear why Spain was chosen, what legal status Abrego Garcia will hold there, or whether his wife and children will join him.
Abrego Garcia, 31, entered the United States illegally as a teenager after fleeing gang threats in El Salvador, where his family ran a pupusa business. He settled in Maryland, married a U.S. citizen and worked as a sheet metal apprentice while raising a family. In 2019, an immigration judge granted him a form of protection known as withholding of removal, which barred the government from deporting him to El Salvador because a gang had threatened his family. He was allowed to live and work in the United States under the supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but never received permanent residency.
In March 2025, federal agents arrested him in Baltimore and deported him to CECOT, El Salvador's maximum-security mega-prison, despite the 2019 order. A government official later described the removal as an "administrative error." He was sent on flights that carried more than 200 Venezuelan and Salvadoran men to El Salvador that month, many of them under the Alien Enemies Act. In El Salvador, he was held first at CECOT and later moved to a lower-security prison in Santa Ana.
His case quickly became a national flashpoint. His wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, sued in federal court in Maryland to secure his return, and in April 2025 the Supreme Court ruled that the government had to "facilitate" his release from Salvadoran custody. Van Hollen flew to El Salvador and met Abrego Garcia that month, while administration officials and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele publicly resisted bringing him back.
The administration returned him to the United States on June 6, 2025, but only after federal prosecutors in Tennessee secured an indictment charging him with human smuggling, tied to a 2022 traffic stop in which he was driving a vehicle carrying other passengers. He pleaded not guilty and his lawyers called the case baseless. In May of this year, U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the indictment, finding that the government had not rebutted a presumption that the prosecution was vindictive and designed to punish him for challenging his deportation. The Justice Department has appealed that ruling.
The gang allegation at the center of the government's case traced back to a 2019 report by Maryland police that was based in part on a confidential informant. The officer who prepared the report was later fired after pleading guilty to misconduct.
After the criminal case collapsed, the administration pressed to deport him to a third country. Officials threatened to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia. Abrego Garcia said he was willing to go to Costa Rica, which had previously agreed to accept him. But in March, ICE official Todd Lyons wrote in a memo that deporting him to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States" and argued for Liberia instead.
The fight over Liberia played out before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis in Greenbelt, Maryland, who had overseen the case since his wrongful removal. On Oct. 6, a hearing on the Liberia plan was canceled minutes after it was expected to begin. Xinis met privately with attorneys for both sides for about 90 minutes, and the parties left without public explanation. The case moved toward a negotiated resolution in the weeks that followed, culminating in this week's departure.
The case drew attention far beyond Maryland because it tested how far the administration could go in removing immigrants quickly and how readily it would comply with court orders to undo its mistakes. Critics of the administration's policies held up Abrego Garcia as an example of due process failures in a mass deportation campaign, while administration officials pointed to the gang and smuggling allegations to argue that he did not belong in the country.
The departure comes weeks after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, giving the president's critics more power to scrutinize his immigration policies from January, when the new Congress is sworn in. Courts are also still weighing challenges to the government's practice of sending deportees to third countries where they have no ties.
His exit to Spain leaves several questions unresolved. The government's appeal of the dismissed smuggling case remains pending, and the sealed agreement has not been made public, so it is not known what commitments either side made or how the deal affects his remaining immigration proceedings. DHS has said he will be barred from returning, while his lawyers are betting on a change in administration.
For now, Abrego Garcia is in Madrid, more than 6,000 kilometers from the family he left in Maryland, under an agreement whose terms neither side has disclosed.

Wrongly deported Salvadoran man arrives in Spain from US
Madrid (AFP) – A Salvadoran man who was wrongly deported from the United States, symbolising President Donald Trump's migration crackdown, celebrated his "freedom" and vowed to "keep fighting" for immigrants after arriving in Spain on Wednesday.
Issued on: Modified:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia's case became a flashpoint in the 2025 political battle over Trump's mass deportations, raising questions about migrants' ability to challenge their orders to leave and the government's willingness to respect court decisions.
"I'm happy and I'm celebrating my freedom," Abrego Garcia told an online press conference hours after landing at Madrid airport on Wednesday, saying "I'm not scared anymore" after taking on Trump's government.
"We won the victory and we will keep fighting for all those people who are going through a trial or an injustice. I want to encourage all those people," Abrego Garcia added.
The Trump administration wanted to deport Abrego Garcia on Tuesday "handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia", his lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg told reporters at Madrid airport, referring to the federal immigration agency.
"And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else," Sandoval-Moshenberg added.
The lawyer explained at the later press conference that Abrego Garcia had chosen Spain because his Salvadoran passport facilitated his entry on the equivalent of a tourist visa.
US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who oversees immigration enforcement, said he was "delighted" that Abrego Garcia "has self-deported from the United States to Spain".
'Reunite this family'
We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement that Abrego Garcia "is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries".
"I have many options for my future. We haven't chosen yet. My family and I will decide the next steps," said Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident and father who is married to an American woman.
"This is a short-term absence from the United States," added Sandoval-Moshenberg. "It is going to be up to the next administration to reunite this family as quickly as possible."
Abrego Garcia was among more than 200 people sent to El Salvador's notorious Center for Terrorism Confinement (CECOT) mega-prison in March of last year.
He had been living in the United States under protected legal status since 2019, when a judge ruled he should not be deported because he could be harmed in his home country.
Justice Department lawyers admitted at the time that Abrego Garcia had been wrongly deported due to an "administrative error".
He returned to the United States last June, with his case becoming a lightning rod for opponents of Trump's efforts to carry out mass deportations.
After his return, Abrego Garcia was detained again and charged with human smuggling in the southern state of Tennessee. The case was later dismissed.
Separate from the criminal proceedings, ICE agents once more detained Abrego Garcia and sought to deport him to Uganda and later Liberia.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia Self-Deports to Spain After Fight
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported to Spain under a removal order, closing a years-long immigration fight that began with his illegal entry and a botched removal to El Salvador, while Democrats cast the exit as freedom from “persecution.”
The Salvadoran national boarded a commercial flight out of the United States after a federal judge told him to leave, and Homeland Security later confirmed he was gone. The New York Post reported the Department of Homeland Security said he “self-deported” late Tuesday night, with Spain as the stated destination and his lawyers telling the New York Times he ultimately plans to go to Mexico.
The departure ends a nearly two-year legal battle that turned Abrego Garcia into a national symbol in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. He is no longer in the United States. That is the result the government sought after months of third-country removal pressure and court fights.
Associated Press reporting said a judge told Abrego Garcia on Tuesday to self-deport. CBS News first reported plans for a commercial flight to Europe. The Washington Examiner reported federal authorities reached an agreement allowing a voluntary departure as soon as Tuesday evening on a commercial flight to Spain.
Fox News reported he landed in Madrid after leaving on a commercial flight and plans to eventually go to Mexico. DHS said he paid for his own ticket, received no self-deportation incentives, left under a removal order, and “will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.”
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin put the administration’s position in plain terms.
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,"
Mullin also said the government had promised voters this man would not stay.
"We promised the American people that this human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator would not remain in our country."
And he added:
"Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans."
Those are the administration’s labels. The criminal human-smuggling case filed after his return was dismissed; the Justice Department had been appealing. Gang membership has been described in coverage as alleged. Readers can weigh the government’s case against the court record.
Abrego Garcia, 31, entered the United States illegally in 2011. He later lived in Maryland with his American wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, and their child. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent back to El Salvador because of a gang threat, and allowed him to live and work here under ICE supervision without residency status.
That protection did not make him a lawful permanent resident. It did not erase the illegal entry. It left him in a supervised gray zone that lasted for years until enforcement caught up.
On March 15, 2025, he was deported to El Salvador and held in CECOT prison. A Trump administration official later called the removal an “administrative error.” The Supreme Court ruled the administration had illegally deported him despite a court order forbidding removal to his native country. He was returned to the United States in June 2025.
Upon arrival he was immediately charged with human smuggling. U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed that case in May. The Justice Department kept fighting the dismissal on appeal while removal planning continued.
After the return, the government pressed third-country options. Abrego Garcia faced potential deportation to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, or Liberia. He argued for Costa Rica. In a March 2026 memo, former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States” and pushed Liberia, citing the resources and political capital spent securing third-country acceptance.
Breitbart reported he avoided forced removal to Liberia by leaving for Spain after a judge allowed him to arrange his own departure. Voluntary departure can still carry a reentry bar when a removal order remains in effect. DHS’s public line is that he is permanently barred.
Photo captions place Abrego Garcia and his wife leaving U.S. District Court in Greenbelt, Maryland, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, and show an earlier federal courthouse appearance in Nashville, Tennessee, on Feb. 26, 2026. The court track ran in parallel with the removal track until the self-deport order closed the U.S. chapter.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., was among Democrats who traveled to El Salvador to visit Abrego Garcia after the first deportation. He framed the Spain exit as a win against the administration.
"I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free, including from this Administration’s constant persecution,"
Van Hollen described him as a “free man.” The senator’s language treats sustained removal efforts as persecution. The other side of the ledger is simpler: a man who entered illegally, lived for years without residency, became the subject of serious DHS accusations, and finally left under a removal order after the government blocked softer landing spots.
Spain is not El Salvador. It is also not an open door back to Maryland. Lawyers say Mexico is the longer-term plan. That is their stated end state. America’s interest was narrower, that he not remain here while officials spent court time, diplomatic capital, and enforcement bandwidth on one contested case.
The administration got him out. Democrats who elevated him now celebrate a departure they once treated as unthinkable cruelty. Illegal entry still has consequences, even when the path runs through years of litigation, a mistaken removal, a Supreme Court remand, a dismissed smuggling case, and a last-minute flight to Madrid.
Borders mean little if the loudest cases never end in exit. This one did.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks from Spain after leaving US: 'My family and I decide our future'
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia speaks from Spain after leaving US: 'My family and I decide our future'
WASHINGTON - Speaking from Spain during a virtual press conference on Wednesday, Nov. 25, Kilmar Abrego Garcia celebrated his voluntary departure from the United States as a victory, declaring that he and his family – rather than federal immigration authorities – chose where to begin their next chapter.
What we know:
Abrego Garcia landed in Spain on Wednesday morning accompanied by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg and advocates from the immigrant advocacy organization CASA, following a nearly two-year legal battle with the Trump administration.
Addressing reporters virtually from Spain alongside Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, Abrego Garcia emphasized that leaving the U.S. on his own terms allowed him to avoid being deported to a country chosen by the government.
"The government did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide our [future]," Abrego Garcia said through a translator. "We haven't decided what's next for my family, but we'll decide what our next steps are going to [be]."
He also offered words of encouragement to other immigrants fighting deportation cases, urging them to "keep your head high just like I did" and pledging to continue fighting alongside them.
What they're saying:
Sen. Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador in 2025 to visit Abrego Garcia while he was being held incommunicado, joined Wednesday's virtual briefing and said he spoke with the Spanish ambassador to the U.S. earlier in the morning to brief her on the case.
"It was great to see Kilmar free and living on his own terms just now from Spain," Van Hollen said during the briefing. "The message for all of us is that it's never wrong to stand up for our Constitution. It's never wrong to stand up for the rule of law. This is a case where the court system did ultimately work, despite the efforts of the Trump administration to trample over our Constitution."
Sandoval-Moshenberg credited Van Hollen's 2025 trip to El Salvador as the turning point in the case, noting that before the senator's visit, Abrego Garcia did not know whether anyone outside the prison knew he was still alive or that people were marching in the streets for his release.
Federal officials offered a sharply different characterization in official posts from the Department of Homeland Security's X account late Tuesday, Nov. 24, repeating unproven allegations against Abrego Garcia and criticizing lawmakers who advocated for him.
"DHS is delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," the agency wrote in a 10:04 p.m. post, calling him a "criminal illegal alien from El Salvador" and adding, "He is not coming back, despite the efforts of sanctuary politicians who spent massive amounts of time and money defending this low-life."
In a follow-up post at 10:43 p.m., DHS added: "To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."
The backstory:
Abrego Garcia, who immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager and lived in Maryland for several years with his American wife and child, drew national attention in March 2025 when he was deported to El Salvador despite a 2019 immigration judge's order barring his removal there due to gang threats against his family.
He was held in El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison before U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials acknowledged in court filings that his removal was an "administrative error." After a judge ordered his return to the U.S., federal officials sought to deport him a second time to an African country.
"The government's goal has been to deport him in shackles on an ICE charter flight to Liberia, and his goal all along has been to depart in the manner and location of his choosing," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
Following his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was indicted on human smuggling charges in Tennessee, though a federal judge dismissed that case in May on grounds of "vindictive prosecution." The Justice Department is appealing that dismissal, with oral arguments scheduled before the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in February.
What we don't know:
Abrego Garcia and his legal team have not disclosed his long-term immigration status in Spain or how his departure will affect the Justice Department's pending appeal in the Tennessee criminal case ahead of February's scheduled arguments.
The Department of Homeland Security said Abrego Garcia cannot come back to the U.S., but his attorneys believe he could legally return under a different presidential administration.
The Source: This article was written using information from a virtual press conference held by Abrego Garcia's legal team and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, official statements from the Department of Homeland Security, the Washington Post, the Associated Press and previous FOX 5 DC reporting.

Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Ábrego García didn't speak to reporters after landing at Madrid's international airport and raised a fist as he entered a van.

We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
Ábrego García would decide where to settle for the next two years to wait out the remainder of the Trump administration, the attorney said. Ábrego García's immigration status in Spain wasn't immediately clear.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back into the U.S.
U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was "delighted" about Ábrego García's departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.
Ábrego García's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.

LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time)
Well, would you look at that. After nearly two years of courtroom battles, congressional outrage, international diplomacy and enough television coverage to make a presidential candidate jealous, Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the United States.
And Democrats are celebrating.
The Salvadoran national, famously dubbed the “Maryland man” in much of the media coverage of his deportation, boarded a commercial flight to Madrid on Tuesday. ABC News reporters observed Abrego Garcia visiting a Customs and Border Protection office at a Washington-area airport before passing through security, reportedly to have his ankle monitor removed.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced that the administration was delighted with the outcome, confirming that Abrego Garcia had self-deported to Spain. Federal officials said he received no financial incentives for leaving and is barred from returning to the United States.
Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador last year to advocate for Abrego Garcia’s release from prison, was considerably less inclined to give the administration any credit. He characterized the departure as a victory over the administration’s treatment of the Salvadoran national.
“This is a victory for due process and our Constitution,” Van Hollen declared on X.
It’s an interesting political predicament. A Democratic senator who made an international trip to champion the return of a man who entered the United States illegally is now celebrating that same man’s departure from the United States.
Apparently, the destination makes all the difference.
There was, of course, a legitimate legal issue with Abrego Garcia’s original deportation. A 2019 immigration ruling prohibited his removal to El Salvador because of threats he faced from a gang in his native country. That protection did not, however, prevent his removal to another country, nor did it confer American citizenship or permanent residency.
The administration acknowledged an error in sending him to El Salvador in March 2025. Following a legal battle that reached the Supreme Court, Abrego Garcia was returned to the United States in June of that year to face federal human-smuggling charges in Tennessee.
Those charges were dismissed in May 2026 after a federal judge found the prosecution had been tainted by a retaliatory motive. The Justice Department is appealing that decision. The administration also alleged that Abrego Garcia was affiliated with MS-13, an allegation he has consistently denied.

Spain has now provided a way out of the impasse, although the full terms of the agreement have not been made public.
Abrego Garcia expressed gratitude to his supporters in a statement following his departure, saying, “I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom.”
But before anyone in Washington starts filing away the paperwork, his legal team has something else in mind.
Attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg indicated that his client’s departure should not necessarily be viewed as permanent. Abrego Garcia’s family remains in Maryland, and his attorney is counting on a change in the White House to help bring him back.
“We don’t expect that to happen under this administration,” the attorney told the Associated Press, explaining that he anticipates a future administration will prioritize reuniting the family.
Abrego Garcia’s departure came just weeks after Democrats secured control of the incoming House of Representatives. The next presidential election, however, is still two years away.

But now, I am not afraid to confront — just as I have already confronted — a government.”
Abrego Garcia was first spotted Tuesday night boarding a commercial flight at Washington Dulles International Airport bound for Madrid.
Flight tracking data indicated his plane landed in the Spanish capital of Madrid early Wednesday.
Abrego Garcia, wearing a dark hooded jacket, was seen at the Washington airport with his wife and brother, as well as lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from immigrant rights group We Are CASA (Central American Solidarity and Assistance).

Before he boarded the flight, Sandoval-Moshenberg said his client was leaving the country his way instead of the way the administration wanted “in shackles” as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainee headed on a government plane to the West African country of Liberia.
Abrego Garcia would return to the United States to open arms and the reunification of his family here following the end of Donald Trump’s presidential term, the attorney said.
His client “has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of a U.S. citizen child,” he added.
He added, “Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice.”
The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.
Abrego Garcia said on Wednesday that this time he left the United States with his freedom, “not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis late Tuesday hailed his departure as a win. “The El Salvadoran man chose to self-deport to Spain — a country that has been wrecked by open border policies. Good riddance,” she said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin used similar language, calling this a matter of self-deportation, and characterized his presence in the United States as focused on an alleged life of crime.
“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported,” he said. “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans.”
Court records in Maryland show that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the U.S. under an agreement with federal authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.
The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the U.S. for years, is married to an American and has a child with her.

“Kilmar and his family are relieved that he is now in a place of his choosing, a free man and living with dignity,” Van Hollen said.
After Abrego Garcia was returned to the U.S. from El Salvador, ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation had been an “administrative error.”
But shortly after his return, Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a 2022 traffic stop for alleged speeding in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.
Abrego Garcia told Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers he was taking the group of nine to a construction job. Authorities there did not pursue charges. A federal judge dismissed the 2025 Department of Justice case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.
The administration continued to pursue Abrego Garcia’s removal, and he was fighting that in a lawsuit that was ongoing prior to today’s news.
Abrego Garcia has been fighting deportation to Liberia, as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. He wanted to go to Costa Rica, according to court records.
Trump and immigration officials alleged Abrego Garcia was an MS-13 gang member, something he denied.
In 2019 records from a loitering case in which he was picked up in a Home Depot parking lot, authorities in Prince George’s County said that Abrego appeared to be an MS-13 member.
They said they made that conclusion based on his clothing (including a Chicago Bulls hat) and tattoos, as well as a proven confidential informant. Abrego Garcia was not formally arrested that day, police said, and they did not have contact with him again. Abrego Garcia’s lawyers later called the evidence of his gang membership “hearsay.”
U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who presided over the Tennessee smuggling case, warned top Trump administration officials to stop making statements about Abrego Garcia that were “exaggerated if not simply inaccurate” and could influence a potential jury.

(Washington Post) Meanwhile: Hundreds of thousands of people who are in the US legally are posed to lose their Medicare benefits. (Washington Post)
Huang
President Trump hinted that he may pardon Jensen Huang during an interview about the NVIDIA CEO’s upcoming testimony to Congress. (New York Post) Huang apologized to the firm’s employees and said he would attend therapy for an hour-and-a-half each day. (NYT) Huang still holds a security clearance despite an affair with a woman thought to be a Chinese spy. (CBS News) The revulsion showed by GOP members of Congress toward Huang’s reinstatement, which Trump says he facilitated, shows that they “may have found an issue on which they can’t bring themselves to take Trump’s side.” (CNBC)
Administration perambulation
Hadrian Automation, a firm with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., may receive a $15 billion loan from the Pentagon. (ProPublica) Three US intelligence agencies, including the CIA, “recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information.” (NYT) The US Army plans to blow up a stockpile of unstable lead azide in Iowa today. (AP) A National Park Service bank account that funds Trump’s DC projects received a $300 million donation in September. The White House won’t say where it came from. (NYT) Convicted Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan filed a motion in civilian court that could delay his planned execution on December 3. (NBC News) Trump awarded Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom. (Washington Sun) The President also conducted the annual turkey pardon, an occasion he used to complain about GOP losses in the midterms. (AP)
Recently on Washingtonian dot com
• Old Ebbitt Grill will soon open Ebbitt House, its first-ever spinoff restaurant, in Reston.
