sources.news_title: A Journey Through the Absurd Hell of Trump’s Third-Country Deportations
sources.text:
The warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner. Instead, the jailer insisted, Rom and his fellow deportees from the United States were “the king’s guests.”
Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa. Then he was made to stand at attention as the country’s national anthem, “Nkulunkulu Mnikati Wetibusiso temaSwati,” reverberated through the halls of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Most meals consisted of a portion of rice splashed with thin broth. It was late 2025, and the weather was warm and wet. For 15 minutes a day, Rom and the other men were allowed to go outside. Before they were locked up for lights out, the anthem played again; thick clouds of mosquitoes kept Rom thrashing all night.
Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene. If I’m a guest, then why am I being held in a prison with criminals? Rom would ask. Why aren’t I allowed to leave? But Rom knew these exchanges with the warden were absurd, like everything else about his situation.
Before the second Trump administration, the practice of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties was a rare and tightly restricted move in US immigration enforcement—reserved mainly for cases where a person simply could not be returned to their nation of origin due to risk of persecution or torture. It has since expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal. Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US. The kingdom of Eswatini, which agreed to take up to 160 migrants for a fee of $5.1 million, is one of them. Some of the other destination countries—the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan—are so violent and unstable that they rank on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.
Often making a spectacle of its own transgressiveness, the administration has steamrolled past public outcry, an investigation by Democratic lawmakers, and a warning from the United Nations about a “cascade of human rights violations” resulting from these removals. At least twice in the past two years, US federal courts have ordered the Department of Homeland Security to stop shipping migrants to third countries with insufficient due process. Both times, the Supreme Court has quickly stepped in to let the administration resume.
In September, during one of those brief, court-ordered pauses in removal flights, DHS general counsel James Percival went on X to publish the most comprehensive figures yet on how many migrants have been affected by the practice. He posted a GIF of Taylor Swift mouthing the words “That’s my husband” and pointing excitedly at her wedding ring. Percival’s caption: “How my wife looks at me when I tell her we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations.”
Rather than slowing down in the face of resistance, in fact, President Trump’s third-country push appears to have inspired imitators. Five European Union countries announced in November that they are working toward a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda. In the past two years, Italy has begun sending asylum seekers to Albania. The United Kingdom quietly sent an asylum seeker to Eswatini earlier this year; the man, originally from Sri Lanka, died last month, the government of Eswatini reported. According to local media, the apparent cause was suicide.
Rom’s lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen—who is himself the child of refugees from Vietnam—predicts that, if the administration keeps getting away with these expulsions, additional wealthy countries will be emboldened to offload their undesirables to poorer nations for a price. “This is going to be the new model for the West, not only for the United States,” says Nguyen, who also represents three other men currently held in Eswatini and Rwanda. “It’s just kind of out of sight, out of mind for these Western countries.”
But as Rom’s experience reveals, some of these removals may rest on little more than bureaucratic fiction. The US claims it has followed due process with every one of the 25,000 migrants deported to unfamiliar lands. “Their own countries say, ‘We do not want them back,’” US attorney general Todd Blanche told Fox News in early October. Yet in Rom’s case—among countless other Kafkaesque details—his own country never even appears to have been asked.
An American in virtually everything but citizenship status, Rom came to the United States as a 3-year-old refugee from Cambodia. Around 1979, his parents fled their home to escape the horrors of the Khmer Rouge, a genocidal regime that seized power in the wake of Richard Nixon’s carpet-bombing of the country. From there, the family went to a Thai refugee camp—where Rom was born in 1982—and then to a resettlement center in the Philippines. As Rom’s father was selling off possessions to raise money for their ultimate move to America, he was killed by roadside thieves. Rom sat by his side after the attack, his mother later told him, trying to wake his father up.
Rom’s first memories of America are of a cramped, dimly lit bedroom in a small apartment in the Bronx, where he arrived with his mother and six siblings in 1985. “There was just one mattress, and we all slept on that,” he says. “It was a new world to us; everything was new.”
Rom and his family had arrived in the middle of the largest resettlement effort in US history. As America’s chimerical war efforts in Southeast Asia faltered in the 1970s, hundreds of thousands of people began arriving in the US from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. Of the nearly 158,000 Cambodians who gained entry between 1975 and 1994, the majority, like Rom and his family, were refugees deeply marked by the atrocities of the Khmer Rouge.
Around 10,000 of them came to be resettled in areas of the Bronx that were blighted by high crime and poverty. Many were placed in dilapidated housing, with limited job opportunities. Rom’s mother, who didn’t speak English, relied on government support checks and whatever extra income she could make sewing and scavenging. As a child, Rom would help her collect cans and carry the overstuffed bags to the grocery store to return for cash.
With the help of an uncle, the family eventually relocated to Philadelphia, where an adolescent Rom was enticed by a newly formed gang—a Cambodian clique within the Crips called the Blue Dragons. “If you don’t want to get bullied,” older members of the gang told him, “you need to link up with us.” Rom was barely a teenager. An older gang member dubbed him Menace, after Dennis the Menace, because he was “funny and bad at the same time.”
By the time he was 18, Rom had done three stints in juvenile detention and was caught in ever-escalating street beefs. At a New Year’s Eve party in 2008, rival gang members jumped him. Rom waited for a day off from his job—caring for abandoned dogs at a local rescue—to seek revenge. He parked outside the gang’s hangout, and when his targets exited, he opened fire from his car. Rom contemplated running when he heard that the police were looking for him but decided against it largely because he had a young daughter. In jail he would be able to see her, even if it was from behind glass. On the lam, he’d have to disappear. He pleaded guilty in April 2010 to multiple charges, including attempted murder.
Rom was a legal permanent resident of the US, a status he had been granted as a refugee. Though refugees are entitled to obtain full American citizenship, Rom had been told he didn’t stand a chance due to his juvenile record, an obstacle that would greatly alter the trajectory of his life.
Under US immigration law since the 1990s, legal permanent residents who commit crimes that qualify as “aggravated felonies”—an expansive and, critics say, somewhat arbitrary legal category—can lose their immigration status and become subject to deportation after they’ve served out their sentences. In a case of what immigrant advocates call “double punishment,” Rom’s conviction for attempted murder meant he would lose his green card. And he knew that in the post-9/11 era, his home country had bowed to US pressure to accept the repatriation of deported Cambodian refugees.
Rom likes to say that prison saved his life. He spent much of his time in lockup reading, exercising, and making cents an hour working in the kitchen to save up for small gifts for his daughter. As he served out his sentence, a generation of shifts in America’s immigration policy flew by—from President Obama’s support of the Dreamers and record-high deportation numbers to Trump’s policy of family separation to Biden’s border crisis to Trump’s return to the White House. But in Rom’s mind, none of that made a difference for him: His fate was already sealed. He was fully prepared to be deported to Cambodia, a country he had never visited, once his sentence was finished.
Rom’s reserved mood as his prison term neared its end confused fellow inmates. “Yo, why are you not happy?” they asked. “You’re about to be released, you made parole.” On November 13, 2024, Rom walked out after serving 15 years. He was immediately transferred to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) holding, where what he believed would be a straightforward process turned into a bewildering journey through the American deportation machine.
From detention, Rom did what he could to hasten the process of his own removal. He frequently called the Cambodian embassy in Washington, DC, seeking information on his departure process. He was told that his questions should be directed to the Department of Homeland Security. Officers in Pennsylvania, he says, had no updates. They told Rom they were swamped by the number of cases they were trying to handle. At one point, they told him he would be deported to Thailand, his country of birth, which he told them was incorrect. After six months of detention, Rom filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he was being unlawfully detained.
He continued to wait for another three months. On September 24, 2025, his daughter’s birthday, Rom saw on a tablet device that his commissary account had been zeroed out. Among ICE detainees, this is a telltale sign that deportation is imminent. The following day, Rom was transferred to Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in Louisiana. He was moved again a few days later to Alexandria, Louisiana, where the airport hums with obscure charter airlines that ferry deportees abroad. He waited there for another 72 hours before he started, again, asking officers what was happening.
At first, they said they didn’t know, a claim Rom found hard to believe. When an officer checked his case on the computer system and then quickly clammed up, Rom’s suspicions grew. Finally they told him to pack up, and Rom caught a look at the immigration paperwork. It listed Eswatini as the country of deportation. Confused, Rom turned to another detainee: “Hey, bro, is Eswatini another ICE facility in Louisiana?” he asked. The man responded that it was in southern Africa.
Rom ran to the phone and made a panicked call to his sister in Las Vegas. She searched online and confirmed that Eswatini was indeed in Africa. Rom asked her to call the Cambodian Embassy. Another detainee’s lawyer suggested the group request “reasonable fear” interviews: US Citizenship and Immigration Services conducts these interviews through their asylum officers to ascertain if a person has a reasonable fear of persecution or torture. Immigration agents seemed amused by the suggestion, Rom says. What could the men be afraid of? they asked. “Y’all a bunch of murderers,” Rom recalls them taunting.
Rom pleaded with the guards. Eventually, one officer told him and the others that if they agreed to be shackled, he would take down their request in writing. They stepped into the restraints, and the officer set about filling out some paperwork. As they sat waiting, their feet and hands in chains, Rom gave the request for a “reasonable fear” interview one last try. “Hey,” he asked, “you think you are going to give us that interview?” He realized it was “all fake” and that the officers never intended to file anything.
One by one, under heavy guard, the men were loaded onto a small airplane. When the door closed it was “like my coffin is closing,” says KV, another deportee on the flight who asked to be identified by his initials because he remains detained. The plane flew from Alexandria to Puerto Rico. The officials accompanying the men gave them no information. They tried, and failed, to disable the small TVs that showed the plane’s flight path.
The plane carried on to Senegal, where they were delayed as officials sought permission to travel onward. “They were basically smuggling us through Africa,” Rom says. When the flight touched down at King Mswati III International Airport early on the morning of October 6, the runway was lined with dozens of armed military personnel. Rom was loaded into a paddy wagon. As the van turned onto a dirt road, Rom was overcome with fear. Oh yeah, they are going to kill us, Rom thought. They’re definitely going to kill us.
Eswatini, a country about the size of New Jersey surrounded almost entirely by South Africa, is the continent’s last remaining absolute monarchy. In April 1973, King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and banned all political parties. The ban remains in place. His son, King Mswati III, took power in 1986, at just 18 years old. Challenges to the monarchy have been met with violence. In June 2021, security forces cracked down on pro-democracy protests, killing 46 people, including two children, according to a government inquiry. Civil society organizations say this is an undercount. A leading human rights lawyer and pro-democracy activist was assassinated at his home two years later. No one has been held accountable for his death.
Eswatini has the highest HIV prevalence rates in the world. Poverty in the country is pervasive. A 2024 report from the US State Department describes Eswatini as having “significant human rights issues,” including torture, media restrictions, and the worst forms of child labor. The king is reportedly married to a cohort of wives and lives a life divorced from his country’s brutal reality. At an April event to mark his 40 years on the throne, he held an extravagant party at a luxury convention center that included a performance by Grammy-nominated singer Davido.
The men, none of whom had committed any crime in Eswatini, were deposited in a high-security area of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Rom’s cell sat behind a large metal door with a barred window painted forest green. When the detainees arrived, the cells were dirty. They asked for cleaning products but were told that none were available. Basic hygiene supplies took four months to arrive. In a dirt courtyard outside, the men had access to a row of concrete sinks to hand-wash their clothes during their 15 daily minutes of outdoor time. One detainee was allowed to retrieve the clothes in the evening.
Rom’s 15-year sentence in the US proved to be a useful experience. He fell back into his workout routine from prison, knocking out 500 pushups a day along with burpees and sit-ups. He read books donated to the prison, churning through the Hunger Games and Twilight series. His lawyer sent him a copy of First They Killed My Father, a memoir about surviving the Khmer Rouge. Rom had expected the weather to cool down at night, but there was little reprieve from the heat. He was given heavy blankets, which meant choosing between sweltering or being swarmed by mosquitoes. He asked jailers the same question he had been asking the guards in the US. “How long am I going to be here?” No one had an answer.
Gradually, the men were granted a few freedoms. They were brought to a mobile store so those without phones could buy them using money from their families. On the way back, they were allowed to eat at KFC and buy two beers apiece. These were the first excursions Rom had taken outside of detention facilities in more than 15 years.
In a post on X, a DHS official had said that the men being deported to Eswatini were “depraved monsters,” and those statements had spread in local media. So Rom smiled and waved, saying hello to the people who stopped to gawk.
The men were permitted to make one phone call a week using WhatsApp. The calls were broadcast in a common room; a prison official would sit nearby, scribbling notes. When Rom wanted to discuss something sensitive with his sister, the two would switch to speaking in Khmer. Local lawyers were barred from visiting. Shortly after Rom was deported, his sister saw a post on Facebook that mentioned Tin Thanh Nguyen, the lawyer in North Carolina. She got in touch, and Nguyen agreed to take Rom’s case.
Thanks to a TV in the common room that was set to the news, Rom was well aware of the controversy surrounding his fellow deportees. He watched a report about one fellow Matsapha inmate from Cuba, Roberto Mosquera del Peral, who had arrived earlier and was on a hunger strike. Each morning, when officers checked Mosquera del Peral’s cell, Rom says, they would shout, mockingly asking if he was still alive.
How Rom and the others came to be trapped in Eswatini is still unclear. According to a report from Reuters, the deal was brokered in February 2025 between Caitlin Piper, a diplomat who was leading the US embassy in the capital of Mbabane, and Russell Dlamini, the country’s prime minister, who sought and received approval from the king. Neither Dlamini nor the acting government spokesperson, Thabile Mdluli, responded to requests for comment. In May, a spokesperson for King Mswati told Reuters that “the king embraced the deal as Eswatini’s contribution to world order.”
Piper has since departed Eswatini. She was most recently based at the US Consulate in Erbil, Iraq, according to social media posts from the consulate. The consulate did not respond to requests for comment on her current position.
In November 2025, more than a month after Rom arrived and four months after the first deportees were deposited at the prison, Eswatini’s finance minister confirmed that he had received a $5.1 million payment from the US. He said the money would be funneled toward Eswatini’s National Disaster Management Agency. The country said it would accept 160 deportees as part of the agreement. The State Department eventually posted a copy of the memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries on May 14, 2025, which confirmed these details. The signature of the US official includes a looping C, but no name is printed underneath. Asked for comment, the Eswatini Press Inquiries Team at the embassy directed questions to the Department of State in Washington. The Department of State did not respond to questions regarding who signed the agreement.
This payment disclosure led the men in detention to charge that they had been trafficked. “You are moving people around, and money is exchanged,” says KV. “So what is that?” If Eswatini got all that money, Rom wondered, why was he having to spend his own on basics like a fan for his cell?
The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC), a human rights NGO, joined several other groups in filing a legal challenge against Eswatini in 2025, aiming to declare the deportation agreement unconstitutional, obtain the terms of the agreement, and secure an order stopping further arrivals until the matter was legally resolved. The initial challenge was dismissed. SALC and the other groups filed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Eswatini in March. (Just weeks before her reported meeting with Eswatini’s prime minister to facilitate the deportations, Piper had addressed an SALC workshop, urging participants “to bring injustice to light, to demand the respect of those in power, to advocate for a world in which our most cherished freedoms are secured.” )
Rom’s personal path to Eswatini appears to have come about through a combination of cruelty and bureaucratic ineptitude. Nguyen points out that Cambodia has been accepting deportees for more than two decades and that the country is generally responsive and professional in issuing the requisite travel documents. He says that the Cambodian government moved to begin rectifying the situation within a week of his contacting them in October 2025.
Nguyen believes that the US erroneously thought Rom should be sent to Thailand, the country of his birth, not citizenship, but never bothered to contact government officials from that country or from Cambodia. Chann Rotana, a spokesman for Cambodia’s foreign ministry, says they also do not understand why Rom was sent to Africa. He adds that the US did not contact the country’s embassy in Washington, DC, regarding Rom’s case before he left the country. Rotana described the deportation to Africa as “strange” and said the embassy only became aware of the situation when Rom’s sister got in touch. Asked about Rotana’s comments, the Department of Homeland Security directed questions to the Department of State, which declined to respond.
“There’s no rhyme or reason as to why any of my clients were picked to go to Eswatini versus the clients that I have who are actually in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia,” Nguyen says. “There’s nothing that makes them distinguishable.”
After an interview with Cambodian officials, Rom’s case for removal progressed while the other men sat hoping for similar developments. When he was cleared to be sent to Cambodia in early February, he requested that he be escorted by a representative from the UN’s International Organization for Migration as a form of insurance. Rom finally arrived in Cambodia on March 26, becoming the second US deportee freed from Eswatini. (The first, a Jamaican man named Orville Isaac Etoria, was deported to Eswatini in July 2025 and repatriated to Jamaica in September of that year.)
When I met Rom in June, at a restaurant in the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh, he was dressed in all black. The sleeves of his polo shirt were taut around his thick, tattooed arms. We met within walking distance of S-21, a Khmer Rouge torture and interrogation center that is now a museum dedicated to the genocide that set his family on its path to America. He is contemplative about his journey and speaks softly.
After arriving in Cambodia, Rom enrolled in a creative writing class, hoping to detail his experience. He was taking teacher training courses, hoping to land a job at an international school, and picked up work fixing air conditioners when he could.
The jarring transition to life in Cambodia was made harder when his older sister—who had been his lifeline in detention—died in July. “Im trying to hold it together,” he texted me. In August, Rom sent a string of messages saying he’d gotten a job teaching English to a rambunctious group of third graders.
Once a week, Rom calls the deportees who remain in Africa. There are more now. A few weeks after Rom and I met, Eswatini announced that it had received a fourth batch of 11 deportees. Another group followed. Thirty-two have been forced to the country in total. KV remains imprisoned. “With the holidays around the corner,” he texted in late September, “it feels I’m wasting my life sitting here for no reason.” It is unclear when he will be released.
The fate of all third-country deportees stands to be clarified in the coming months. After at least twice granting the Trump administration temporary stays to keep deporting migrants to third countries, the US Supreme Court will start hearing oral arguments on the ultimate legality of the practice in December.
Shortly after he arrived in Cambodia, Rom noticed that Kuenene, his warden at Matsapha, had added him as a contact on Telegram and WhatsApp. Another Eswatini official requested to connect on Facebook and follow Rom on Instagram. Rom accepted some of the invitations and declined others; he couldn’t tell why they were trying to befriend him. Maybe Kuenene wanted to keep tabs on what Rom might say publicly. “He was one of those guys that tell you what you want to hear, smile at your face, make you believe that he is the most supportive guy in the world, and then he will stab you in the back,” Rom said. “I didn’t trust him.” Before he was released, Rom told the guards and other deportees that he might return to Eswatini to visit as a tourist. In reality, he has no intention of ever returning. One visit as a royal guest was enough.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Self-Deports to Spain, DHS Says He Will ‘NEVER’ Return › American Greatness
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the illegal immigrant from El Salvador whose removal case became a rallying cry for Democrats, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday, Fox News reported.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Abrego Garcia flew to Spain on a commercial flight. His attorneys told The New York Times he ultimately plans to go to Mexico. Two sources said a federal judge in Maryland had ordered him to leave the country by Tuesday. That order is under seal, and the terms of his release were not immediately clear.
The Department of Homeland Security said Abrego Garcia paid for his own ticket and did not receive any financial incentives through the administration’s voluntary self-deportation program.
“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” Mullin said. He called Abrego Garcia a “human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator” and said the administration had promised he would not remain in the country. “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans,” Mullin added.
DHS said Abrego Garcia “departed the United States pursuant to a removal order” and declared, “He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.” The department rejected descriptions of him as a Maryland resident, calling him “a criminal illegal alien from El Salvador” and a threat to public safety, and faulted “sanctuary politicians” for defending him.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who visited Abrego Garcia while he was held in El Salvador, praised the outcome. “A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen said. He said Abrego Garcia was now leaving as “a free man” and “unharmed and with dignity,” and claimed the administration “was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will.”
Abrego Garcia entered the country illegally more than a decade ago and lived in Maryland with his wife and children. Immigration authorities detained him in March 2025. He was then mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in the CECOT maximum-security prison, even though a court order barred his removal there because of the risk of gang persecution. Federal officials at one point sought to send him to several African countries.
He was later brought back to the United States to face human smuggling charges stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. He pleaded not guilty, and a judge later dismissed the charges.
The administration has maintained that Abrego Garcia is a member of the MS-13 gang and has pointed to a 2021 protective order his wife sought against him over domestic violence allegations. Democrats rallied to his side despite those suspected gang ties.

sources.news_title: Abrego Garcia will voluntarily leave US, ending 20-month legal ordeal
sources.text:
Abrego Garcia will voluntarily leave US, ending 20-month legal ordeal
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
Kilmar Abrego Garcia will voluntarily leave the United States for Spain on Tuesday night, appearing to bring to an end a tortuous, 20-month saga that began when the Trump administration wrongfully deported him to a prison in his homeland of El Salvador.
Abrego Garcia’s decision to leave for Spain came as he faced the prospect that the administration might decide his fate for him and deport him to Liberia.
A Salvadoran native, Abrego Garcia was working and living in suburban Maryland with his family when federal agents grabbed him off the streets in March 2025 and, days later, flew him to El Salvador in a clear-cut violation of a court order that barred him from being sent there.
As he fought his expulsion from overseas at every level of the U.S. legal system, including the Supreme Court, he became a symbol of resistance to President Donald Trump’s aggressive — and, at times, error-prone — deportation agenda.
When the justices ordered the Trump administration to facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return to the United States, the Justice Department brought him back from El Salvador, but only as part of an effort to indict him on charges of taking part in a human smuggling conspiracy.
A federal judge ultimately determined that those charges were a vindictive abuse of prosecutorial power and that the effort to pursue a criminal case against Abrego Garcia was essentially a way to comply with the Supreme Court’s instructions while also saving face.
His lawyers took note of his long ordeal in a statement issued Tuesday night.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” the lawyers said. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The Justice Department did not respond to a message seeking comment.
Abrego Garcia’s tribulations, which unfolded in three separate cases heard by multiple sets of judges, presented a major test of Trump’s demand for the mass deportation of immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. It was also a flashpoint pitting Trump’s expansive view of executive power against the fundamental tenets of judicial review and the rule of law.
“The government is asserting a right to stash away residents of this country in foreign prisons without the semblance of due process that is the foundation of our constitutional order,” one conservative jurist, J. Harvie Wilkinson III, wrote in April 2025 in a ruling affirming the order to facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return to the United States.
For months, the court battle over Abrego Garcia’s wrongful deportation was marked by an extraordinary level of obstinance by the Justice Department, which over and over dragged its feet in complying with court orders. Making the department’s stonewalling even more unusual was that officials admitted that the administration had erred in sending Abrego Garcia to the Salvadoran prison, but repeatedly refused to fix its own mistake.
The first judge to hear the case, Paula Xinis, of U.S. District Court in Maryland, became so frustrated that at one point she opened a contempt investigation into the department lawyers handing the matter, accusing them of shattering the traditional bonds of the trust that the government has long enjoyed in court.
“This has been the process from Day 1,” Xinis said during a hearing in July 2025. “You have taken the presumption of regularity and you’ve destroyed it in my view.”
Outside the courtroom, Trump and some of his most senior aides treated Abrego Garcia’s case less as a legal proceeding and more, at times, as an opportunity to demonize a man who had very publicly fought his expulsion. The president and members of his Cabinet often assailed Abrego Garcia as a terrorist and a member of the violent street gang MS-13 even though judges repeatedly questioned the evidence that lay behind those accusations.
Trump personally accused him of belonging to MS-13, citing an image in which the gang’s name had been superimposed above a series of tattoos on Abrego Garcia’s knuckles. Turning the case into a White House spectacle at one point, Trump held a news conference in the Oval Office at which Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said he would never let Abrego Garcia leave his country, saying that to do so would be akin to sending “a terrorist into the United States.”
All the while, Abrego Garcia languished in a prison known as CECOT, which was designed to hold terrorism suspects. He claimed that he was beaten, deprived of sleep and psychologically tortured during nearly three months in custody there.
His ordeal continued even after he was brought back from El Salvador to face charges in Nashville, Tennessee, of having acted as a driver for a smuggling ring that transported immigrants without legal status across the country.
Those charges were dismissed in their entirety in May by Judge Waverly D. Crenshaw Jr., who determined that the case had only been brought to punish Abrego Garcia for having challenged the efforts to deport him. In his ruling, Crenshaw singled out Attorney General Todd Blanche for criticism, saying that prosecutors had reawakened a dormant investigation into Abrego Garcia at his request and that of his top deputies.
Even as it sought to prosecute Abrego Garcia in Nashville, the Justice Department didn’t give up on its efforts in Maryland to deport him, a double-tracked approach that seemed at times to confuse both Crenshaw and Xinis, who oversaw the parallel cases.
Moreover, the department had trouble settling on a country that it wanted to deport him to, and, more important, that would receive him. Officials floated plans to send Abrego Garcia to Uganda, Ghana and the small African nation of Eswatini, but failed in the end to get permission from the governments of those countries to take him.
Ultimately, they tried to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia, but his lawyers fought that move in court, saying that their client would willingly deport himself to Costa Rica if the government allowed it. That case ended in an impasse — that is, until Abrego Garcia agreed to fly to Spain on Tuesday night.

sources.news_title: Ábrego García, Salvadoran national mistakenly deported by US, arrives in Spain and enjoys 'freedom'
sources.text:
MADRID (AP) — Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the U.S., potentially ending a defining saga of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child and had lived in Maryland for years, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and was deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain follows months of legal wrangling as he battled the Trump administration’s drive to deport him to Africa.
“The U.S. government may be the most powerful government in the world, but justice can still prevail,” Ábrego García said in a statement released Wednesday. “In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”
Ábrego García, who’s in his 30s, migrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He didn’t speak to reporters after landing at Madrid’s international airport and raised a fist as he entered a van. But at a virtual news conference later, he thanked his supporters and said, “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom.”
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, called the move “a temporary departure.”
“Mr. Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen spouse and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
Sandoval-Moshenberg thanked Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Ábrego García when he was sent back to El Salvador, for his advocacy and said that visit was a turning point in the case. “Without that," Sandoval-Moshenberg said, “I have no doubt that El Salvador would have continued to stonewall.”
Van Hollen said he spoke to Ábrego García and his wife before they departed the U.S. He reflected on his visit to see Ábrego García in El Salvador, saying, “We had no idea whether Kilmar Ábrego García was alive or dead.”
He said he was glad the Trump administration didn’t succeed in carrying out its vendetta against Ábrego García because he stood up for his rights. “They wanted to leave him to rot there, to rot there for the rest of his life," he said.
Ábrego García would decide where to settle for the next two years to wait out the remainder of the Trump administration, Sandoval-Moshenberg said. Ábrego García’s immigration status in Spain wasn’t immediately clear.
U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who presided over Ábrego García’s long-running immigration proceedings in Maryland, ordered the case’s dismissal on Wednesday after receiving confirmation that he had left the U.S.
The court also unsealed an order that Xinis signed last Friday to spell out the terms of his “unimpeded” departure. In the order, Xinis said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.”
The judge, in turn, set Tuesday as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.
The order didn’t address why the government had changed its position on him leaving the U.S. to a country of his choice.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn’t receive any incentives and won’t be allowed back into the U.S.
U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Ábrego García’s departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.
Ábrego García’s deportation in early 2025 came as Trump, a Republican, was ramping up his immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.
Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by the U.S. Congress, the Trump administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.
Ábrego García was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

sources.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García left the United States for Spain on Tuesday under a deal that allowed him to depart voluntarily rather than be forcibly deported to Liberia, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal and ABC News.
A federal judge permitted the 31-year-old Salvadoran national to arrange his own departure, and his lawyers were able to head off the administration’s plan to send him to Liberia. ABC News reported that he was seen boarding a commercial flight to Madrid from a Washington-area airport.
The precise terms of Tuesday’s arrangement have not been made public, and immigration officials note that voluntary departure can still trigger a bar on reentry if a removal order remains in place. It remains unclear whether Ábrego García will be able to return to the United States, though federal law does allow a future administration to grant him permission to apply for reentry even in cases where someone would otherwise be barred.
Ábrego García entered the country illegally as a teenager and settled in Maryland. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that officials could not send him to El Salvador after finding he faced a credible threat there.
The Trump administration deported him to El Salvador in March 2025 anyway, in violation of that order, and he was held at the country’s CECOT prison. The Supreme Court subsequently directed the administration to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.
He was brought back to the United States in June 2025 after federal prosecutors in Tennessee secured a two-count human-smuggling indictment against him. In May, a federal judge dismissed that case, ruling that prosecutors had pursued the charges to punish Ábrego García for challenging his earlier deportation. The Justice Department has appealed that ruling.
Trump administration officials have accused Ábrego García of belonging to the MS-13 gang, an allegation he has denied. His wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, sought a protective order in Maryland in 2021, alleging that he had punched and scratched her. She later said she decided not to pursue the case and that the couple underwent counseling.
Before settling on Liberia, immigration officials had considered sending Ábrego García to Uganda, Eswatini, or Ghana. His lawyers pushed instead for Costa Rica and obtained a court order temporarily blocking his removal while they challenged the government’s chosen destination. According to CBS News, U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis issued a sealed order on the Friday before his Tuesday flight to Madrid.
His attorney, Sean Hecker, confirmed the trip to Spain to the Washington Post. Reuters, meanwhile, reported that his lawyers told the New York Times he ultimately intended to travel on to Mexico.

sources.news_title: Wrongly deported Salvadoran man voluntarily leaving US: Senator
sources.text:
Washington: A Salvadoran man who was wrongly deported from the United States, placing him at the center of a row over President Donald Trump's crackdown on migrants, is leaving the country, according to a US senator who visited him after his deportation.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was among more than 200 people sent to El Salvador's notorious Center for Terrorism Confinement (CECOT) mega-prison in March of last year.
Abrego Garcia had been living in the United States under protected legal status since 2019, when a judge ruled he should not be deported because he could be harmed in his home country.
He returned to the United States last June, with his case becoming a lightning rod for opponents of Trump's efforts to carry out mass deportations.
While detained at CECOT, Abrego Garcia was visited by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who said in a statement Tuesday that the 31-year-old was now leaving the United States of his own accord.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Admin wanted to leave Kilmar to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement. "Today, he is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man -- unharmed and with dignity."
Van Hollen's statement did not specify where Abrego Garcia was headed, but US media reported he was going to Spain.
CBS News, citing multiple US officials familiar with the matter, said he was planning to fly to Spain on a commercial flight on Tuesday. It said the exact nature of his arrangements and the conditions of his departure were unclear.
Abrego Garcia's lawyer did not respond to a request for comment.

sources.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García voluntarily left the United States for Spain on Tuesday under a deal that spared him forced deportation to Africa and could affect whether he can return under a future president.
The administration got Ábrego García out of the country, and his lawyers kept immigration authorities from sending him to Liberia. ABC News saw him board a commercial flight to Madrid at a Washington-area airport.

Ábrego García entered the United States illegally as a teenager and settled in Maryland. An immigration judge barred officials from sending him to El Salvador in 2019 after finding he faced a threat there.
The Trump administration sent him there in March 2025 in violation of that order, and he was held at the country’s CECOT prison. The Supreme Court directed the administration to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.
The administration brought him back in June 2025 after Tennessee federal prosecutors obtained a two-count human-smuggling indictment. A federal judge dismissed the case in May, ruling that prosecutors had brought the charges to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The Justice Department appealed.
Trump administration officials accused Ábrego García of belonging to MS-13, which he denied. She later said she decided against pursuing the case and that the couple went to counseling.

Ábrego García’s lawyers pushed for Costa Rica and secured a court order temporarily blocking his removal while they fought the administration’s choice. CBS News reported that U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis issued a sealed order Friday, four days before he boarded the flight to Madrid.

sources.news_title: KILMAR ABREGO GARCIA IS NO LONGER A 'MARYLAND MAN' — He's Self-Deporting to Spain Today
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally roughly 15 years ago and whose case Democrats turned into a national political cause, boarded a commercial flight from the Washington, D.C. area to Madrid, Spain, on Tuesday, ABC News reported after observing him at the airport.
Multiple U.S. officials told CBS News that Abrego Garcia was expected to leave the country Tuesday on a commercial flight. ABC News reported that before clearing security, Abrego Garcia entered a Customs and Border Protection office at the airport, in part to have his ankle monitor removed — a device federal immigration officers fitted him with more than a year ago when he was returned to the United States.
The terms of his departure have not been publicly disclosed. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has presided over his civil litigation in Maryland, issued an order Friday that remains under seal. Fox News reported that the departure followed a directive from the judge that he leave by Tuesday.
The Associated Press reported that Abrego Garcia was leaving voluntarily for Spain, which is governed by socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. According to 100PercentFedUp, his attorneys say Mexico is where he ultimately plans to go. For months, the administration and Abrego Garcia's lawyers had fought over which country would receive him — he expressed a willingness to go to Costa Rica while the administration explored Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia.
The Saga
The Trump administration deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison in March 2025 as part of its immigration crackdown. The administration later acknowledged the removal was an administrative error, because a 2019 immigration judge had granted him withholding of removal to that particular country.
After the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Abrego Garcia should be returned to the United States, he was brought back last June to face human smuggling charges in Tennessee tied to a 2022 traffic stop. He pleaded not guilty, and a federal judge dismissed the indictment on vindictive-prosecution grounds. The Justice Department kept the case alive and in August the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Tennessee appealed the dismissal to the Sixth Circuit.
No member of Congress invested more political capital in the case than Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), who flew to El Salvador in April 2025 and met with Abrego Garcia personally.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice. I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration's constant persecution."
Van Hollen also claimed the administration was "forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation."
An Instagram post indexed Tuesday showed a photo captioned as a conversation with Abrego Garcia and his wife; the post's caption was not a transcript and the account did not release its contents. It circulated as the departure reports broke.
What Was Alleged
Central to the case were allegations of Abrego Garcia's ties to MS-13, which predated his deportation by six years, according to RedState. Abrego Garcia has denied gang membership. He never received permanent legal status after entering the country illegally as a teenager. The 2019 immigration ruling protected him from removal to El Salvador — it did not grant him a right to remain in America permanently or bar the government from pursuing removal to another country.
It is not yet known whether the criminal appeal in the Sixth Circuit will continue now that he has left the country, or whether Spain's government was consulted on the sealed arrangement.
Spain's foreign ministry did not immediately comment on the arrival, according to wire reporting Tuesday.
Our Take
So ends the strangest immigration story of Trump's second term — not with a courtroom vindication for the men who spent two years insisting Kilmar Abrego Garcia was a victim of American cruelty, but with a one-way ticket to Madrid on a commercial flight he walked onto himself.
Remember what Democrats actually demanded. They demanded he be returned to the United States — and a federal judge obliged, releasing him from ICE detention onto American streets to await trial. They demanded due process, and he got it, including a dismissed indictment and an appeal still grinding through the Sixth Circuit. What they never demanded was the obvious thing: that a man in the country illegally, facing gang allegations he denies, eventually leave. Van Hollen flew to El Salvador for a photo op but could not bring himself to fly to Spain with his constituent.
The administration's March 2025 removal to El Salvador was an error — the government said so itself, and a 2019 order specifically barred sending him there. That error is why this dragged on for two years and gave the Left its martyr. But the outcome Tuesday is the correct one: Abrego Garcia is out of the United States, voluntarily, without the spectacle of a forced removal Democrats could fundraise off. He will not be in Maryland. He will not be in a Tennessee courtroom. He will be in Spain.
Patriots should mark what this cost: congressional trips, sealed orders, years of court time — all to remove a man who was removable from day one. The lesson is not that the system worked. It is that the system took two years to do what should have taken two weeks. Ask your representatives why the deportation of a single Salvadoran national required the Supreme Court, and why the answer from the Left was never "leave" — only "stay."
And notice how quiet the mainstream media will be about this self-deportation. Doesn't fit their narrative.

After the US government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped.
The Trump administration had continued its attempts to deport him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
Footage shared with the BBC's US partner CBS shows an ICE ankle monitor being removed from Ábrego García upon his arrival in Spain. He told the outlet that he was leaving the US "happy" and "with his freedom".
Ábrego García's lawyer said in a statement his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".
"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.
"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed to the BBC that Ábrego García had left the country, decrying him as a criminal.
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Ábrego García has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Mullin said in a statement, adding "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorise innocent Americans".
The Trump administration claims Ábrego García is a member of the MS-13 gang, which he has denied.
In a post on social media, the Department of Homeland Security wrote that Ábrego García had left the country "pursuant to a removal order".
"He paid for his own flight and received no incentives," the DHS said on X. "He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."
Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities.
A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by one of the country's criminal gangs.
In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.
The administration acknowledged that he had been wrongly deported and brought him back to the US, where he was set to face human trafficking charges.
A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle with the government over further efforts to deport him.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, while the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and offer him legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point, the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

In short:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia will self-deport to Spain amid a struggle with the US government to prevent his deportation to Africa.

A Salvadoran national who the US mistakenly deported to his home country last year is self-deporting to Spain, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the case.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia became a focal point in the US's immigration debate after the deportation error and had been fighting a second deportation to Africa.
Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen said Mr Abrego Garcia was a "free man" who was travelling to a country of his choice.
"I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration's constant persecution," he said.
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager.
Department of Homeland Security officials had proposed deporting Mr Abrego Garcia to a series of African countries.
The judge in that case told Mr Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, local time.
Attorneys who represented Mr Abrego Garcia in the Maryland immigration proceedings and a criminal case in Tennessee did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
A spokesperson for We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Mr Abrego Garcia and his family, declined to comment.
"Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe," spokesperson Jossie Flor Sapunar said.
In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that Mr Abrego Garcia could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family.
The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an "administrative error".
Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump's administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee.
A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department's pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Mr Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation.
The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.
Mr Abrego Garcia had argued that if he was going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him.
But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Mr Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States".
Mr Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the US had spent government resources and political capital negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals, Mr Lyons wrote.
The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the US signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
The case took an unusual turn on October 6, 2026, when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether US Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Mr Abrego Garcia to Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Mr Abrego Garcia.
When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was cancelled.
The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation.
Mr Abrego Garcia's attorney said the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

sources.news_title: After being mistakenly deported to El Salvador and returned to the U.S., Kilmar Abrego García boards a flight to Spain under a sealed departure agreement
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego García boarded a flight from the Washington, D.C., area to Madrid on Tuesday, beginning a voluntary departure from the United States after a nearly two-year legal battle that started with his mistaken deportation to a notorious Salvadoran prison.
ABC News observed Abrego García boarding the flight. Before going through security, he entered a Customs and Border Protection office at the airport, where a source said he was to have an ankle monitor removed. The monitor had been issued after he returned to the United States. Details of the arrangement allowing him to leave remain sealed. The Associated Press reported that a person familiar with the matter said a judge had instructed him to self-deport Tuesday; The Washington Post reported that his lawyers and government attorneys negotiated the agreement.
The departure followed months of disputes over where the U.S. could send him. Abrego García had said he was willing to go to Costa Rica, while the Trump administration pursued removal to several African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia. A hearing on the government's effort to deport him to Liberia was abruptly canceled in October after Judge Paula Xinis met privately with attorneys. Sealed filings, including an order, were entered in the case last week.
Abrego García was born and raised in El Salvador, where his family ran a pupuseria. Court records say the Barrio 18 gang extorted the family and threatened to kill him and relatives. His family sent him to the United States as a teenager to live with his older brother. He later settled in Maryland with his U.S. citizen wife and children, and worked as a sheet metal apprentice.
In 2019, an immigration judge granted him "withholding of removal," ruling that he could not be sent to El Salvador because he faced a clear probability of persecution there. That protection did not give him permanent residency or prevent deportation to every country. It barred his removal to El Salvador, leaving the government able to seek another destination through immigration proceedings.
The Trump administration deported him to El Salvador on March 15, 2025, despite that order. The government later acknowledged the removal was illegal and attributed it to an "administrative error." Officials also alleged that Abrego García belonged to MS-13, a claim he denied. Public reporting traced the allegation to a 2019 Maryland police gang report based partly on a confidential informant. The Washington Post reported that the officer who prepared the report was later fired after pleading guilty to misconduct, and that the county had stopped using the field-interview form amid concerns about its reliability.
Abrego García was held at El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, as part of the Trump administration's deportation campaign. In April 2025, the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody and ensure his case was handled as it would have been had he not been improperly removed. The court did not reinstate the original deadline for his return, and directed a lower court to clarify the order. He was brought back to the United States on June 6, 2025, after federal prosecutors indicted him in Tennessee on human-smuggling charges.
Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego García pleaded not guilty. In May 2026, U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the indictment, finding that the government had failed to rebut a presumption of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department appealed, so the case remains subject to further court proceedings.
The public details of Abrego García's departure agreement, including what it means for his immigration proceedings, have not been disclosed. ABC News reported that he was in the process of self-deporting to Spain; his longer-term plans have not been made clear publicly.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego García arrives in Spain, ending deportation battle
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego García arrives in Spain, ending deportation battle
Key takeaways:
- Kilmar Abrego García leaves U.S. for Spain
- Agreement reached between Abrego García’s attorneys and government lawyers
- Abrego García challenged illegal deportation to El Salvador gang prison
- Sen. Chris Van Hollen praised agreement for respecting due process
MADRID — Kilmar Abrego García has arrived in Spain after departing the United States on his own, ending a 20-month legal saga over the fate of a Salvadoran migrant whose case became a symbol of the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign.
His commercial flight took off from Virginia late Tuesday, delayed by several hours because of mechanical difficulties.
It landed at 11 a.m. local time, which is 5 a.m. in Washington, D.C.
Abrego García’s departure from the U.S. is the result of a negotiated agreement between his attorneys and government lawyers, said two people briefed on the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the details of that arrangement have not been made public.
The agreement comes after months of officials insisting that Abrego García, 31, should be deported to Africa.
His lawyers maintained that choice was meant to punish Abrego García for successfully challenging both his illegal deportation to a notorious gang prison in El Salvador last year and separate criminal charges filed against him in Tennessee after multiple courts ordered his return.
“Kilmar Abrego García has left the United States a free man,” his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said in a statement. “The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world.”
Abrego García traveled Tuesday to a government office at Dulles International Airport in Fairfax, Virginia, about 25 miles from the White House.
Officials removed the GPS tracking device that the government had affixed to his ankle nearly a year earlier.
Abrego García’s group smiled and snapped selfies after passing through security without incident and taking the tram to his gate.
But after boarding, the plane had mechanical difficulties, and the passengers had to disembark to go to one gate and then another.
Uniformed airport officers appeared to trail Abrego García wherever he went.
Abrego García kept a low profile, with his head bowed and covered in a hooded sweatshirt. He was surrounded by a group of advocates, his wife and his brother. But he said he was upbeat.
“I’m happy,” he said in a brief interview in Spanish.
As the plane was taxiing down the runway, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a social media post that Abrego García had “self-deported.”
“This is a temporary departure,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said, noting that Abrego García will eventually have some options to return to the United States because he is married to a U.S. citizen and they have a child together who is also a U.S. citizen.
His wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, has sponsored Abrego García for legal U.S. residency, which would put him on a path to citizenship. But under federal law, he cannot return for 10 years because of the length of time he lived in the U.S. without legal status.
His attorneys do not expect the federal government to waive that penalty while Trump is in office. Another administration might, especially because of his wife and child, his attorneys said.
“We expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration’s choice. He has a lot of options, and he is still determining them.”
Since he was brought back to the U.S. in June 2025, Abrego García had said he was willing to voluntarily leave for Costa Rica. But U.S. immigration officials refused.
Abrego García’s attorneys secured a court order temporarily barring his removal from the U.S. while their legal fight played out.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of his attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement Tuesday evening. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The battle over Abrego García’s fate has, for many critics, come to epitomize what they view as some of the worst aspects of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts.
Abrego García lived for years in Maryland with his wife and children. He had been working as a sheet metal apprentice. He has said he came to the U.S. from El Salvador as a teenager to flee death threats from the Barrio 18 gang.
Because of that gang threat, a U.S. immigration judge in 2019 barred officials from deporting Abrego García to El Salvador. The Trump administration arrested and deported him there anyway last year; multiple courts concluded the deportation was a violation of the 2019 order.
Still, for months, officials resisted court orders – including one from the Supreme Court – to facilitate Abrego García’s return to the U.S. Officials publicly derided him as an “animal,” a gang member and a domestic abuser – accusations he repeatedly denied.
He was only brought back to the U.S. last year after federal investigators reopened a previously shuttered human smuggling investigation and secured a two-count indictment against him.
A federal judge tossed that case in May, ruling that prosecutors had improperly pursued charges to punish Abrego García for challenging his deportation in court. The Justice Department appealed. A department spokesperson did not immediately return requests for comment Tuesday on what his planned departure might mean for that case.
While that legal battle played out, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement continued to threaten Abrego García with deportation to an ever-changing series of countries in Africa.
In March, the Trump administration said it had settled on Liberia, one of several nations that have agreed to accept non-native deportees from the U.S. The Justice Department asked a federal judge in Maryland to lift an order she imposed last year barring Abrego García’s removal while he challenged that destination in court.
Abrego García’s attorneys contend he had designated Costa Rica as his preferred country of removal, and the Central American nation’s previous administration indicated they would welcome him.
However, a new Costa Rican government recently said it had not received a fresh request and would have to consider whether to admit him.

sources.text:
Abrego Garcia flies to Spain, ending 20-month deportation battle with Trump administration
Kilmar Abrego Garcia stands outside U.S. District Court in Greenbelt in December 2025 beside his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, left, and Lydia Walther-Rodriguez with CASA, after a federal judge ruled he was allowed to remain free. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.
The move ends 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents in March 2025 and erroneously deported to his native country.
In a statement late Tuesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department was “delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” fulfilling the administration’s promise that he “would not remain in our country.”
But in a statement released shortly after midnight Wednesday morning, the immigration advocacy group We Are CASA said Abrego Garcia had “cleared his name of the Trump administration’s bogus charges against him and walked out of the United States a free man.”
The statement said Abrego Garcia was accompanied on a commercial flight by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney and a We Are CASA representative. It said they were met at the airport by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who removed the ankle monitoring bracelet Abrego Garcia has had to wear since courts ordered him released from detention and returned home to Beltsville.
Abrego Garcia said in the statement that “justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”
“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom. I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight,” his statement said. “I feel good. I feel confident. I believe everything will be okay because God is with us.”
Abrego Garcia’s deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.
Top ICE official elaborates on plan to send Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Liberia
Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.
It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S. and said he was “relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution.”
“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”
Neither Van Hollen nor We Are CASA specified Abrego Garcia’s destination, but news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.
The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Uganda, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.
A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there. But it did not prevent the government from trying to send him to a third country – an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.
Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.
“Mr. Abrego Garcia had been asking permission to leave the country since August 2025,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of his attorneys, in the We Are CASA statement. “The Trump Administration held him and refused to allow him to depart, first in an ICE detention center for five months and then on electronic monitoring in Maryland for almost a year, all the while insisting on deporting him to a series of African countries. That retaliatory deportation campaign has now come to an end.”
Abrego Garcia was eventually returned from El Salvador in June 2025, but was immediately arrested and charged by ICE with human smuggling in Tennessee. Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding in Tennessee, when Abrego was driving an SUV carrying a number of Latino men.
Abrego Garcia was let go with a warning after the traffic stop and the case was closed. But federal officials reopened it two years later and charged Abrego Garcia with human smuggling as soon as he was returned from El Salvador.
Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued the flimsy charges were mere pretext to punish their client after he beat the administration in court. A federal judge in Tennessee agreed in May and tossed the case out as a vindictive prosecution and an abuse of government power.
It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen’s statement said.
Ama Frimpong, We Are CASA’s chief of legal services and another of Abrego Garcia’s attoenrys, called it “a victory that Kilmar gets to choose what comes next.”
“He is choosing where and how to lead his life. He is beginning this new chapter with the safety, freedom, and dignity he fought to reclaim,” Frimpong said in the statement. “That victory belongs first to Kilmar; to Jennifer, whose voice carried their family’s fight across the country; and to their family, who endured more than any family should.
— This story was updated Wednesday morning to include comments from the Department of Homeland Security and We Are CASA, and details of the Tennessee charges against Abrego Garcia.
