sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national whose case became a focal point in the immigration debate after he was mistakenly deported to his home country last year, is self-deporting to Spain Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen described Abrego Garcia as a “free man” and said he is traveling to a country of his choice.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he said in a statement.
The move came as Abrego Garcia was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. The judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday.
Attorneys who represented Abrego Garcia in both the Maryland immigration proceedings and his criminal case in Tennessee didn’t immediately respond to messages seeking comment. A spokesperson for We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family, declined to comment.
“Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe,” said the spokesperson, Jossie Flor Sapunar.
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump’s administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.
Abrego Garcia had argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”
Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third country nationals, Lyons wrote. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
The case took an unusual turn Oct. 6, 2026, when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.
When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was canceled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation. Abrego Garcia’s attorney said only the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia is leaving US after Trump-era deportation saga
sources.text:
Trump-era deportation saga comes to close with Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving US voluntarily
Salvadoran immigrant at center of high-profile legal battle over president’s mass deportation efforts is leaving for Spain
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Donald Trump’s administration has reached an agreement to let Kilmar Abrego Garcia leave the U.S. voluntarily, ending a nearly two-year legal battle over the fate of a Salvadoran immigrant whose story has been at the center of the president’s mass deportation campaign.
He boarded a commercial flight to Spain on Tuesday night, according to his legal team.
Abrego Garcia’s case has been a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s efforts to rapidly arrest and deport tens of thousands of people from the country despite legal safeguards and humanitarian protections that the president has also eroded since returning to the White House.
The administration has spent the last year trying to deport Abrego Garcia a second time — including to Liberia — after the government unlawfully deported him to a brutal prison in his home country, triggering the high-profile legal battle for his return.
“Kilmar Abrego Garcia has left the United States a free man,” his attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg said in a statement to The Independent.
“This is a temporary departure,” he added. “Mr. Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”
But where he goes from here “will be his choice, not the administration's choice,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added. “He has a lot of options, and he is still determining them.”
The Independent has requested comment from the Department of Homeland Security.
Abrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years after fleeing gang violence in El Salvador and entering the U.S. illegally as a teenager. An immigration judge blocked the government from deporting him to his home country in 2019.
But last year, federal agents abruptly deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison where he says he endured torture and “severe” abuse for several weeks before he was transferred to a separate jail.
Government officials admitted in court that his removal was due to an “error,” and several federal judges and a unanimous Supreme Court ordered the administration to “facilitate” his return.
The government spent weeks battling those orders while White House officials launched a barrage of public attacks against him and declared that he would never again step foot in the country.
He was returned to the U.S. last June — only to face allegations that he illegally moved other immigrants across the country. He pleaded not guilty.
A federal judge later dismissed the criminal case against him after finding that the administration unlawfully targeted him as part of a smear campaign.
“Objective evidence” has shown that federal prosecutors only brought charges against Abrego Garcia after he won his lawsuit challenging his arrest and removal, the judge ruled.
The administration has, at the same time, tried to deport him to at least five different countries, including four in Africa, and refused to let him leave the country for Costa Rica.
In a memo issued in March, ICE’s then-acting director Todd Lyons argued that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”
In April, the administration “analyzed and eliminated all other options” from the table and settled on Liberia as “a final country of removal,” despite his own attempts to voluntarily remove himself to Costa Rica.
Government lawyers argued in court documents that the U.S. has expended significant political capital and entered “high-stakes” and “extensive negotiations” to send him to Liberia.
But the judge overseeing his deportation case had blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement from re-deporting or detaining him, noting earlier this year that the government has made “one empty threat after another to remove him to countries in Africa with no real chance of success.”
Both sides were scheduled to discuss his case at a hearing in October, but U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis abruptly ended the hearing after she met privately with attorneys in her chambers.
Judge Xinis issued an order in the case on November 20 but it remains sealed.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who traveled to El Salvador in an attempt to secure Abrego Garcia’s release from prisons there, said his constituent is now “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
“While the Trump administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday night.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution,” he added. “This is a victory for due process and our Constitution.”

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national mistakenly deported as part of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, was leaving the U.S. voluntarily for Spain on Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Abrego Garcia’s expected departure, which would come after months of legal wrangling over his case, could bring to a conclusion what has become a defining saga of the second Trump administration’s mass deportations agenda.
A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport by Tuesday, according to the person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.
Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March, 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while he was pressing for his release from a Salvadoran mega-prison, described Abrego Garcia as a “free man” and said he is travelling to a country of his choice.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he said in a statement.
Abrego Garcia’s deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport a million people annually. Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, increasing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.
Attorneys who represented Abrego Garcia in both the Maryland immigration proceedings and his criminal case in Tennessee didn’t immediately respond to messages seeking comment. A spokesperson for We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family, declined to comment.
“Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe,” said the spokesperson, Jossie Flor Sapunar.
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump administration asks military base near Chicago to support immigration enforcement
The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
Facing public pressure and a court order, U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration brought him back in June, 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.
Abrego Garcia had argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”
Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third country nationals, Lyons wrote. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
The case took an unusual turn Oct. 6 when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.
When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was cancelled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation. Abrego Garcia’s attorney said only the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego García arrives in Spain, ending deportation battle with U.S.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. and arrives in Spain
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. and arrives in Spain
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, his team and the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.
Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid early Wednesday morning, alongside his wife, an American citizen, and his lawyer, a representative for the family told CBS News. Video of his departure from the U.S. showed his ICE ankle monitor being removed.
CBS News was first to report Abrego Garcia's plans earlier Tuesday.
Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, flew to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday night.
"I can now breathe freedom," he said during a virtual press conference on Wednesday.
Abrego Garcia, speaking from Spain, said he and his family, not the U.S. government, will decide their "next steps."
"The government did not decide where my story continues," he said. "My family and I decide our future."
Abrego Garcia traveled out of the U.S. with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez, his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from We Are CASA, the U.S. advocacy group that has been helping him and his family.
Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia entered Spain with his Salvadoran passport and has a pathway to becoming a lawful permanent resident of the U.S., though that would require a waiver from the State Department that is unlikely to be granted by the current administration.
Still, he said the Trump administration did not succeed in its efforts to deport him to Liberia, as it sought to do.
"Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines," Sandoval-Moshenberg added. "Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus. And there's really no other way to see this other than, you know, Mr. Abrego Garcia's decision to hold strong throughout the last two years."
Trump administration officials touted Abrego Garcia's departure.
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said. He reiterated the Trump administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia belongs to a gang — which his legal team has denied — and said he now "cannot terrorize innocent Americans."
In a social media post late Tuesday night, the Department of Homeland Security wrote: "To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."
The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the U.S. last year to face criminal charges.
Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.
But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, DHS said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.
Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly canceled. The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.
But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.
In an order Wednesday, Xinis officially closed Abrego Garcia's case and dissolved the injunctions that she had previously imposed after "having received confirmation" that he had left the U.S.
The judge also directed a separate order issued Friday to be unsealed. That order, now publicly available, stated that Abrego Garcia would leave the U.S. by Tuesday and directed the Trump administration to "take all steps within their control to ensure [Abrego Garcia's] unimpeded departure and transit from the United States — to include the lifting of any detainer, lookout, alert, hold, or other records — that would cause Petitioner to be detained, questioned, or denied boarding on any aircraft."
The judge also directed the Trump administration to remove Abrego Garcia's GPS ankle monitor before boarding the plane taking him out of the country, and reiterated that the Department of Homeland Security could not interfere with his travel to the airport and departure from the U.S.
Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.
But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.
In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.
The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive.
The Justice Department has appealed that decision, and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February.

sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Is No Longer a ‘Maryland Man.’ He Is Leaving the U.S. Today
sources.text:
Remember the “Maryland man” who became the subject of an international political controversy, inspired congressional Democrats to travel to El Salvador, and occupied a ludicrous amount of court time?
Well, he's reportedly heading to Spain. And sadly, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) is not going with him.

The terms of Abrego Garcia's departure have not been publicly disclosed. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has presided over his civil litigation in Maryland, issued an order Friday that remains under seal.
If the reported arrangements go through, it would bring one of the more peculiar political sagas of President Donald Trump's second term substantially closer to an end.
And what a saga it has been. Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally approximately 15 years ago, became a political cause célèbre for Democrats after the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador in March 2025.
Perhaps no member of Congress invested more political capital in Abrego Garcia's case than Sen. Van Hollen, who flew to El Salvador in April 2025 and met with him personally.
Now Kilmer Garcia and Senator Van Hollen are sharing drinks. Why was he released? https://t.co/sOONo1zQIV
— Natalie Winters (@nataliegwinters) April 18, 2025
The administration acknowledged that Abrego Garcia's removal to El Salvador was an administrative error, as an immigration judge had granted him withholding of removal to that particular country in 2019.
The Associated Press also reported Tuesday that Abrego Garcia was leaving voluntarily for Spain, which is governed by socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
For months, the Trump administration and Abrego Garcia's attorneys had been fighting over which country would receive him. Among the most sinister aspects of the Abrego Garcia affair were his alleged ties to the notorious MS-13 gang. Those allegations predated his deportation by six years. In 2019, Maryland police documented information from a confidential informant identifying Abrego Garcia as a member of the gang.
Immigration Judge Elizabeth Kessler subsequently denied his request for release on bond, writing that the determination of his gang membership “appears to be trustworthy” and was supported by other evidence in the record. The Board of Immigration Appeals upheld the bond decision.

The Trump administration brought Abrego Garcia back to the United States in June 2025 to face those charges. He pleaded not guilty.
In May of this year, a federal judge dismissed the indictment on the grounds of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department has appealed that ruling, with oral arguments scheduled for February. So, while Abrego Garcia may be leaving the country, his legal saga isn't necessarily over.
Now, after nearly 20 months of litigation, international diplomacy, congressional intervention, and media coverage, Abrego Garcia is reportedly boarding a commercial flight out of the United States.
Next stop: The MS-13 sanctuary state of socialist Spain. If anything, Kilmar Abrego Garcia has given Americans an extended lesson on just how hard it is to remove one illegal alien.
But, at the end of the day, the credibly accused gang member is leaving the United States, showing us all that it is possible for the trash to take itself out.

sources.news_title: Abrego Garcia Leaves the U.S. for Spain, Ending His 20-Month Deportation Fight
sources.text:
Abrego Garcia Leaves the U.S. for Spain, Ending His 20-Month Deportation Fight
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation became a flashpoint in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday under an agreement to depart voluntarily.
Reporters saw Abrego Garcia board a flight from a Washington-area airport to Madrid, ABC News reported. Before going through security, he stopped at a Customs and Border Protection office, in part to have his ankle monitor removed, a source told the network.
One of his attorneys, Sean Hecker, told The Washington Post that Abrego Garcia was leaving for Spain Tuesday evening. Two people briefed on the case described a negotiated agreement for the 31-year-old to depart voluntarily.
The terms have not been made public. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who oversees his civil case in Maryland, issued an order Friday that remains sealed, CBS News reported. The judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, the Associated Press reported.
Abrego Garcia entered the U.S. illegally as a teenager and settled in Maryland, where he has an American wife and child. In 2019, an immigration judge barred his removal to El Salvador because a gang had threatened his family.
Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 and sent him to El Salvador’s CECOT prison anyway, which an official later called an “administrative error.” The administration has said he is a member of MS-13, which he denies, according to ABC News.
After the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release, he was returned in June 2025, but only after a Tennessee grand jury indicted him on human smuggling charges stemming from a 2022 traffic stop. He pleaded not guilty.
A federal judge dismissed those charges in May, finding the prosecution was vindictive. The Justice Department has appealed, and arguments before the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals are set for February, according to CBS News.
Spain, Not Liberia
The administration spent months trying to send Abrego Garcia to a third country, naming Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and most recently Liberia, the Associated Press reported. He had asked to go to Costa Rica, which had agreed to take him.
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, wrote in a March memo that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States,” according to the AP.
The case went quiet in October, when a hearing on whether ICE could detain and deport him to Liberia was abruptly canceled. Several sealed filings followed, including a sealed order last week.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who traveled to El Salvador to meet Abrego Garcia after his deportation, said in a statement that the administration was “forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him.”
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen said.
A spokesperson for We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported his family, told the AP: “Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe.”

Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and a judge later dismissed the charges in May.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.

For the past year and a half, he has been fighting for the right to leave the United States to the country of his choice," said Abrego Garcia's lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, in part. "The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world."
Sandoval-Moshenberg went on to say that he believes this will be only temporary and that as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of another U.S. citizen, Abrego Garcia will have options to come back under a different administration.
Some Trump administration officials celebrated the agreement, with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin saying in a statement, in part, "We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain."
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis also said in a statement, in part, "The El Salvadoran man chose to self-deport to Spain—a country that has been wrecked by open border policies. Good riddance.”

News4 reached out to the Justice Department for comment and has not heard back.

A hearing for Abrego Garcia that was expected to determine whether he would be deported to Liberia was abruptly canceled last month for reasons that were not immediately clear.
The government was moving to vacate a preliminary injunction put in place by U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis preventing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from detaining and deporting Abrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia. His legal team was seeking to make the injunction permanent. The judge left previous orders in place last December and ordered him released from custody.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a lawyer for Ábrego Garcia, told media outside the courthouse simply that the hearing could not happen and that an update to the case would be posted on the court docket in the next few days. He shed no light as to why the hearing was cancelled.
Abrego Garcia argued that if he were to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to accept him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States," because the U.S. had expended resources and political capital negotiating with Liberia to accept third-country nationals.
The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
Abrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family.
Abrego Garcia was then sent to a mega-prison in El Salvador known as CECOT, which activists say is rife with abuses and where inmates are packed into cells and never allowed outside. ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.”
Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump's Republican administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May 2026, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. sources.news_title: Kilmar Abrego García will leave U.S. for Spain to avoid deportation
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego García will leave U.S. for Spain to avoid deportation
Federal authorities have agreed to let Kilmar Abrego García depart the United States voluntarily, according to two people briefed on the matter, ending a 20-month legal saga over the fate of a Salvadoran migrant whose case became a symbol of the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign.
One of his attorneys, Sean Hecker, said Abrego was scheduled to leave for Spain on Tuesday evening.
Hours before that, he traveled to a government office at Dulles International Airport in Virginia, about 25 miles from the White House. Officials removed the GPS tracking device that the government had affixed to his ankle nearly a year ago and cleared him through security checkpoints.
Then, after Abrego and other passengers had boarded their flight to Spain, the airline announced mechanical difficulties with the plane. Passengers disembarked and were waiting for a replacement aircraft as of 7:30 p.m.
Abrego was surrounded by his wife and a handful of advocates, and kept his head bowed and covered with a the hood from his sweatshirt. He chatted quietly with his group as he waited to board another plane.
His departure from the United States is the result of a negotiated agreement between his attorneys and government lawyers, said the two people briefed on the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the details of that arrangement have not been made public.
The agreement comes after months of officials insisting that Abrego, 31, should be deported to Africa.
His lawyers maintained that choice was meant to punish Abrego for successfully challenging both his illegal deportation to a notorious gang prison in El Salvador last year and separate criminal charges filed against him in Tennessee after multiple courts ordered his return.
Since he was brought back to the United States in June 2025, Abrego had said he was willing to voluntarily leave for Costa Rica. But U.S. immigration officials refused.
Abrego’s attorneys secured a court order temporarily barring his removal from the United States while their legal fight played out.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” Hecker said in a statement Tuesday evening. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The battle over Abrego’s fate has, for many critics, come to epitomize what they view as some of the worst aspects of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts.
Abrego lived for years in Maryland with his wife, a U.S. citizen, and children. He had been working as a sheet metal apprentice. He has said he came to the United States from El Salvador as a teenager to flee death threats from the Barrio 18 gang.
Because of that gang threat, a U.S. immigration judge in 2019 barred officials from deporting Abrego to El Salvador. The Trump administration arrested and deported him there anyway last year; multiple courts concluded the deportation was a violation of the 2019 order.
Still, for months, officials resisted court orders - including one from the Supreme Court - to facilitate Abrego’s return to the United States. Officials publicly derided him as an “animal,” a gang member and a domestic abuser - accusations he repeatedly denied.
He was only brought back to the U.S. last year after federal investigators reopened a previously shuttered human smuggling investigation and secured a two-count indictment against him.
A federal judge tossed that case in May, ruling that prosecutors had improperly pursued charges to punish Abrego for challenging his deportation in court. The Justice Department appealed. A department spokesperson did not immediately return requests for comment Tuesday on what Abrego’s planned departure might mean for that case.
But while that legal battle played out, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement continued to threaten Abrego with deportation to an ever-changing series of countries in Africa.
In March, the Trump administration said it had settled on Liberia, one of several nations that have agreed to accept non-native deportees from the United States. The Justice Department asked a federal judge in Maryland to lift an order she imposed last year barring Abrego’s removal while he challenged that destination in court.
Abrego’s attorneys contend he had designated Costa Rica as his preferred country of removal, and the Central American nation’s previous administration indicated they would welcome him. However, a new Costa Rican government recently said it had not received a fresh request and would have to consider whether to admit him.
Both sides were set to argue the matter at a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis on Oct. 6. As that proceeding began, Xinis met privately with attorneys in her chambers. She abruptly canceled the hearing once they emerged. For weeks, little surfaced about developments in the case.
After Abrego’s departure plans were reported Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) praised the agreement as one that allowed him to leave the U.S. “unharmed and with dignity.” Van Hollen visited Abrego during his time in prison in El Salvador last year.
“The Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free - including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”

sources.news_title: ‘Maryland Man’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Self-Deport to Spain over One Year After Tennessee Star Reporting Led to Federal Charges: Report
sources.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has reportedly agreed to self-deport to Spain, ending a legal battle with the Trump administration that began when he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025.
Citing U.S. government officials familiar with the matter, CBS News and The New York Times reported that Abrego Garcia will leave the country for Spain on Tuesday, despite his attorneys previously asking the federal government to send him to Costa Rica.
Prosecutors working on the criminal case against Abrego Garcia originally raised the possibility of removal to Costa Rica during failed plea deal negotiations last year. After the U.S. State Department obtained diplomatic assurances from Costa Rica as part of the abortive plea deal negotiations, Abrego Garcia identified the nation as his preferred destination, despite also claiming he feared persecution or torture upon his arrival.
While Abrego Garcia will reportedly self-deport to Spain, The Times reported that his legal team indicated he intends to eventually settle in Mexico.
Abrego Garcia sued the Trump administration after he was deported to El Salvador, which courts have determined violated a 2019 final deportation order that contained a withholding of removal provision stating he was forbidden from being sent to Guatemala. Judges have since determined the withholding-of-removal order actually referred to El Salvador.
Following the March 2025 deportation to El Salvador, the Trump administration initially said it had no mechanism to force President Nayib Bukele to surrender return a citizen of El Salvador to the United States.
Abrego Garcia was only returned to the country after a grand jury returned an indictment accusing him of participating in a human smuggling conspiracy, which followed April 2025 reporting by The Tennessee Star of his November 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee.
During the traffic stop, Abrego Garcia was revealed to be driving without a valid license and transporting nine individuals who lacked identification and did not speak English. The Star was the first to confirm with the Tennessee Highway Patrol (THP) that troopers were instructed to release Abrego Garcia by the “Biden-era FBI.”
Prosecutors later confirmed that an agent with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) reviewed The Star’s reporting and forwarded her findings to the federal prosecutor for the Middle District of Tennessee, ultimately leading to the charges against Abrego Garcia.
The criminal case against Abrego Garcia was dismissed earlier this year by U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama. He dismissed the case, claiming the DOJ did not defeat the presumption that the administration was vindictively prosecuting Abrego Garcia.
The Trump administration has appealed, and earlier this month, the DOJ submitted a brief to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals urging the appellate court to reverse Crenshaw’s decision, arguing the judge was wrong to consider potential vindictiveness so early in the case.
Last year, The Star received the Dao Prize for Best Local Journalism for its reporting on Abrego Garcia.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving the US, self-deporting to Spain
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was returned to the U.S. after being mistakenly deported to a Salvadoran mega-prison, is self-deporting to Spain, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.
Earlier Tuesday, ABC News observed Abrego Garcia boarding a flight from a Washington, D.C.-area airport to Madrid, Spain.
His flight took off late Tuesday, four hours after his originally scheduled departure time.
The flight was deplaned twice because of mechanical issues, and its departure gate was changed three times.
ABC News observed Abrego Garcia with his wife, brother, attorney and members of a local immigrant advocacy group.
In a statement that repeated claims of domestic violence and human smuggling against Abrego Garcia, among other allegations, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed the move.
“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” Mullin said.
Abrego Garcia's departure marks a major development nearly two years after the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison as part of its ongoing immigration crackdown.
Prior to his boarding the flight to Spain, ABC News observed Abrego Garcia enter a Customs and Border Protection office at the airport before going through airport security -- in part, a source said, to have his ankle monitor removed after it was issued by federal immigration officers when he was returned to the United States over a year ago.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, where Abrego Garcia and his family live, said in a statement that the Trump administration was "forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation."
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag. Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice," said Van Hollen, who traveled to El Salvador to meet with Abrego Garcia following his deportation. "I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free -- including from this Administration's constant persecution."
Abrego Garcia, who had been living in Maryland with his wife and children, was deported in March of last year to CECOT -- despite a 2019 court order barring his deportation to that country due to a fear of persecution -- after the Trump administration claimed he was a member of the criminal gang MS-13, which he denies.
After the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Abrego Garcia should be returned to the United States, he was brought back to the U.S. last June to face human smuggling charges in Tennessee, after which U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis released him from ICE detention while he awaited trial.
In May, a federal judge dismissed the criminal indictment against him, finding that the government's investigation had been tainted "with a vindictive motive."
In October, Judge Xinis, who has been overseeing Abrego Garcia's immigration case, abruptly canceled a hearing on the matter. Last week, several sealed filings were filed in the case, including a sealed order.
In court filings, the Trump administration had been pushing for Abrego Garcia's deportation to a third country in Africa. Government officials had previously named the countries of Liberia, Uganda and Eswatini as potential destinations for removal.
